entry.title: OData MCP Proxy - Interactive UI views in your MCP server
entry.content:
Introduction

In my previous blog post I showed how to build your own SAP MCP server in minutes with the odata-mcp-proxy npm package: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/build-your-own-sap-mcp-server-in-minutes-with-odata-mcp-proxy/ba-p/14348685

That gave you tools. Tools return JSON, the model reads the JSON and tells you what it found. That works fine for "how many subaccounts do I have", it works a lot less fine for "show me my subaccounts". At some point you don't want a summary of your data, you want to see it.

So the proxy now supports interactive UI views. You declare them in the same API config file next to your APIs, you write a self-contained HTML page and the proxy registers it as an MCP tool that returns a rendered widget instead of a text blob. No custom code required. Just configuration.

Before I start, credit where it is due: @Marian_Zeis  and @mike_zaschka showed what MCP-UI can do in their session at reconnect. I went home from that session wanting this in my own MCP server, so thanks to both of them for the inspiration 🙂

In this blog post, I'll walk you through what this looks like, how it works under the hood and how I used it in my BTP MCP server.

Problem

MCP-UI (https://mcpui.dev) already existed and it is a nice specification: a tool result can carry a ui:// resource with an HTML page and the host renders it in an iframe next to the chat. The problem is not the specification, the problem is everything around it.

To get one interactive view into my BTP MCP server I had to:

  • write my own entry point, because the proxy had no hook to register extra tools per session
  • copy the transport and session wiring out of the proxy into that entry point
  • deep-import from odata-mcp-proxy/dist/... to reuse the OData clients
  • fetch and aggregate the BTP API responses server-side
  • assemble the HTML, inject the data and wrap it in createUIResource

That is what my btp-mcp-server project looked like: a server.js of 170 lines that mostly duplicated the proxy bootstrap and a src/ui folder with four more files doing data acquisition, aggregation and template assembly. It worked, I got my dashboards, but every other consumer of the proxy would have to copy the same 650 lines to get their own. That is not a feature, that is a fork.

Next to that, the moment the proxy released a new version I had to re-check whether my copied bootstrap still matched.

Solution

So I moved all of it into the proxy itself. Since version 1.1.2 the API config file accepts a top-level ui array and each entry becomes a read-only MCP tool that:

  1. validates its input parameters
  2. fetches its data sources concurrently through the same OData clients and destinations as the generated entity tools, including the caller's JWT
  3. inlines the shared CSS/JS partials into the HTML template
  4. bakes the payload into the page and returns it as an mcp-ui embedded resource

The default/min/max inputs, the date built-ins, the pagination and the select trimming below came a bit later, in 1.2.0.

The result on my side: server.js deleted, src/ui deleted, around 650 lines of application code gone. There is now no server-side application code left in the btp-mcp-server project at all, only a config file and a folder of HTML, CSS and browser JavaScript. Looking at that folder for the first time felt a bit strange 🙂

This is the entire package.json of the BTP MCP server today:

{
  "name": "btp-mcp-server",
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "description": "MCP server for SAP BTP administration with interactive MCP-UI dashboards",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "odata-mcp-proxy --config btp-admin-api-config.json",
    "build:btp": "mbt build",
    "deploy:btp": "cf deploy mta_archives/btp-mcp-server_1.0.0.mtar"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC",
  "dependencies": {
    "odata-mcp-proxy": "^1.3.0"
  }
}

One dependency and three scripts.

What is MCP-UI?

If you are new to it: MCP-UI is to an MCP tool what a Fiori app is to an OData service. The service can perfectly return you the raw entities, but nobody wants to read those, so you put a UI on top. MCP-UI does the same for a tool result: next to the text result, the tool returns a small self-contained web page and the host (Claude or any other mcp-ui capable client) renders it in an iframe in the conversation.

The page can talk back to the host. A click in the view can ask the host to call another tool, which is how the cross-navigation in my dashboards works: you click "Locations map" in the overview and the host calls the UI_GeomapDashboard tool, which renders the next view.

The proxy enables the MCP Apps adapter on every view, so the same widget runs on MCP Apps hosts like Claude and on classic mcp-ui hosts without you doing anything for it.

How it works

An overview of what happens on a tool call:

 model calls UI_SubaccountsOverview
        |
        v
 [1] validate inputs        (inputs -> zod schema)
        |
        v
 [2] fetch data sources     (concurrently, via the shared ODataClient + destination + JWT)
        |
        v
 [3] assemble template      (partials inlined into the HTML)
        |
        v
 [4] inject payload         ("__DATA__" replaced by the JSON)
        |
        v
 tool result: short text summary + ui:// resource + structuredContent

Two things are worth calling out here.

The first one is that the data acquisition reuses the existing OData clients. A UI view is not a second way into your backend, it is the same destination, the same OAuth token caching and the same principal propagation as the generated entity tools. If a user is not allowed to read subaccounts, the view doesn't show them either.

The second one is that the server stays dumb on purpose. It fetches, it inlines and it substitutes one token. All aggregation, grouping and charting is the template's job, in the browser. I did consider adding some kind of aggregation syntax to the config, but every version of that I wrote on paper ended up being a small programming language in JSON. So the raw responses go to the template and the template shapes them.

The configuration

Every view is one entry in the ui array:

Field

Required

Description

tool

yes

The MCP tool name. Registered read-only.

description

yes

Tool description for the LLM. This is what makes the model pick the view over the plain data tool.

uri

yes

The ui:// resource URI. The template is also registered as an MCP resource here, so hosts that pre-fetch templates can use render-data delivery.

template

yes

HTML template file, path relative to the config file.

inputs

no

Tool parameters, compiled into the input schema. Supports type, required, default, min, max and description.

data

no

Named data sources, fetched concurrently. Supports optional, paginate and select.

partials

no

Literal token to file map, inlined into the template before the data is injected.

frameSize

no

Overrides the mcp-ui preferred frame size (default ["100%", "760px"]).

 

This is the geomap dashboard of my BTP MCP server as an example:

{
  "tool": "UI_GeomapDashboard",
  "description": "Show a world-map dashboard plotting where all BTP subaccounts run (data-center locations, sized by subaccount count, with drill-down).",
  "uri": "ui://btp-mcp-server/dashboard-geomap",
  "template": "ui/dashboard-geomap.html",
  "data": {
    "subaccounts": {
      "api": "cis-accounts",
      "path": "subaccounts",
      "select": ["guid", "displayName", "region", "state", "usedForProduction"]
    },
    "datacenters": {
      "api": "cis-entitlements",
      "path": "globalAccountAllowedDataCenters",
      "optional": true
    }
  },
  "partials": {
    "/*__SHARED_CSS__*/": "ui/_shared.css",
    "/*__SHARED_JS__*/": "ui/_shared.js",
    "/*__REGIONS__*/": "ui/_regions.js",
    "__WORLD_PATH__": "ui/_world-path.txt"
  }
}

A few notes on this one:

  • api refers to the name of an API in the same config file, so a single view can combine data from several BTP APIs. Here the subaccounts come from the Accounts service and the data-center list from the Entitlements service.
  • optional: true makes a failing source resolve to null instead of failing the whole tool call. The data-center list is nice to have, it should not break the map when the entitlement API is not reachable.
  • select keeps only the listed fields of each item. This is not only about the browser, the payload also travels back to the model as structuredContent, so trimming it saves tokens.
  • partials is a plain token to file replacement. My five views share the same CSS and helper JS, the world outline is a separate file because it is a very long SVG path which I didn't want inside the HTML.

Placeholders in a path

{param} expands to a validated tool argument, URL-encoded:

"subaccount": { "api": "cis-accounts", "path": "subaccounts/{subaccountGUID}" }

Next to that there is a small closed vocabulary of built-ins for the things that came back in every view I wrote: dates and paging.

Placeholder

Expands to

{$now:FMT}

The current UTC time

{$monthsAgo(N):FMT}

The first of the month, N months back

{$daysAgo(N):FMT}

N days back

{$offset} / {$pageSize}

The page position, only on a source with a paginate block

 

FMT is yyyymm (202608), date (2026-08-11) or iso. N can be an integer, the name of a tool input or that name with one integer offset. That last form exists because a reporting window that includes the current month needs months-1 and I really didn't want to add expressions to the config for it. So one offset is the only arithmetic there is:

"usage": {
  "api": "uas-reporting",
  "path": "monthlyUsage?fromDate={$monthsAgo(months-1):yyyymm}&toDate={$now:yyyymm}"
}

{$monthsAgo} snaps to the first of the month on purpose, otherwise a yyyymm window would shift depending on the day you ask the question.

Pagination

The SCIM Users API returns 100 users per request, so the users dashboard needs paging. This can be done with a paginate block instead of a loop in code:

"users": {
  "api": "xsuaa-scim",
  "path": "Users?startIndex={$offset}&count={$pageSize}",
  "paginate": {
    "strategy": "offset",
    "pageSize": 100,
    "maxItems": 500,
    "itemsPath": "resources",
    "totalPath": "totalResults"
  },
  "select": ["userName", "emails", "origin", "active", "groups", "meta.created", "lastLogonTime"]
}
  • strategy: offset is 1-based (SCIM startIndex), skiptop is 0-based (OData $skip)
  • pageSize: items per request, exposed as {$pageSize}
  • maxItems: hard cap on the accumulated items
  • itemsPath: where the items live in the response, auto-detected when you leave it out
  • totalPath: the field with the backend's total count, when it reports one

A paginated source hands the template a normalized { items, total, truncated, pages } object. The truncated flag turned out to be the useful part: my old server-side paging loop just stopped at the cap and the dashboard happily showed 500 users as if that was everything. Now the view says it is showing a capped subset.

The template

A template is a normal, self-contained HTML page. The only thing the proxy does to it is replacing the token "__DATA__" with the JSON payload:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<style>
/*__SHARED_CSS__*/
</style>
</head>
<body>
<script id="btp-data" type="application/json">"__DATA__"</script>
<div id="app" class="wrap"></div>
<script>
/*__SHARED_JS__*/
 
bootView(function (payload, app) {
  var subs = asArray(payload.data.subaccounts);
  // build your DOM here
});
</script>
</body>
</html>

The token is quoted, so the raw template stays valid JavaScript and you can open it in a browser with a fixture while developing. The payload has the shape { view, params, data } where data contains your named sources. < is escaped as \u003c in the injected JSON, so a subaccount with a <script> in its description can never close the surrounding tag.

Cross-navigation from inside the view is a postMessage to the host:

function uiTool(toolName, params) {
  window.parent.postMessage({
    type: 'tool',
    messageId: 'btp-' + (++__msgSeq),
    payload: { toolName: toolName, params: params || {} }
  }, '*');
}

Which is what the buttons in the header of my overview call:

h('button', { class: 'btn', onclick: function () { uiTool('UI_GeomapDashboard', {}); } }, '🌍 Locations map')

Result

Five views declared in one config file, this is the subaccounts overview with the stat tiles, the per-region chart and the searchable table:

The UI_SubaccountsOverview view rendered in the chat

Clicking "Locations map" makes the host call the geomap tool, which plots the data-center locations of all subaccounts:

The UI_GeomapDashboard view, reached by clicking "Locations map"

Clicking a row in either view opens the detail view with the entitlements of that subaccount, from where you can go back to the overview or to the map. The consumption and the users & roles dashboards are one click away in the header of the overview. All of that is one ui array and a folder of HTML files.

The full BTP OData MCP Proxy is here: https://github.com/lemaiwo/odata-mcp-proxy and can be used as a plugin from npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/odata-mcp-proxy

The full BTP MCP server is here, it is a good example to start from using the OData MCP Proxy from because there is nothing else in it: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server

Conclusion

Adding a UI to an MCP server used to mean forking the server. It is now a section in the config file next to your APIs. You still write the HTML yourself, which I think is the right split: the interesting part of a dashboard is the dashboard, not the plumbing to get the data into it.

The UI machinery is loaded lazily by the way, so if your config has no ui section the @mcp-ui/server dependency never even gets imported.

Contributions and feedback are welcome, both repositories are public.

entry.title: OData MCP Proxy - How to add a UI view to your own MCP server
entry.content:
Introduction

In my previous blog post I introduced the interactive UI views of the odata-mcp-proxy: a ui section in your API config that turns an HTML page into an MCP tool: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/odata-mcp-proxy-interactive-ui-views-in-your-mcp-server/ba-p/14469713 

That post explained what it does. This one is the hands-on part.

Thanks again to @Marian_Zeis  and @mike_zaschka , whose session at reconnect put me on this track in the first place.

In this blog post, I'll show you exactly how to add your first UI view to your own MCP server, step by step, starting from a config that only has data tools. We're going to build a small products overview, add a parameter to it, share the styling between views and finally let the view navigate to another view.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18 or higher
  • An MCP server project based on odata-mcp-proxy. If you don't have one yet, start with this post first: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/build-your-own-sap-mcp-server-in-minutes-with-odata-mcp-proxy/ba-p/14348685
  • odata-mcp-proxy version 1.2.0 or higher. The ui section itself exists since 1.1.2, but the defaults, the date built-ins and the pagination we use further on need 1.2.0

Your starting point is a project with just these files:

my-mcp-server/
├── package.json
├── api-config.json
└── .env

And an api-config.json with at least one API in it:

{
  "server": {
    "name": "my-mcp-server",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "description": "My custom MCP server"
  },
  "apis": [
    {
      "name": "my-api",
      "destination": "MY_DESTINATION",
      "pathPrefix": "/api/v1",
      "entitySets": [
        {
          "entitySet": "Products",
          "description": "product entities",
          "category": "master-data",
          "keys": [{ "name": "Id", "type": "string" }],
          "operations": { "list": true, "get": true, "create": false, "update": false, "delete": false }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Problem

With this config you get a Products_list tool. Ask your assistant for your products and you get a paragraph of text describing them or a JSON dump. That is fine for a question about one product, it is not fine when you want to look at all of them, sort them by price and click through to the details.

What we want instead is a real table in the chat, rendered from live data, without writing a server.

Solution

The proxy can do this from configuration. A UI view is three things:

  1. an HTML file in your project
  2. an entry in the ui array of your config, saying which data it needs and which template renders it
  3. nothing else

Let's have some fun.

Step 1: Update the package

This can be done with npm:

npm install odata-mcp-proxy@latest

You can validate if this was successful by checking the version in your package.json, it needs to be 1.2.0 or higher:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "odata-mcp-proxy": "^1.3.0"
  }
}

Step 2: Create the template

Create a folder ui next to your config file and add a file ui/products-overview.html. A template is a normal, self-contained HTML page. There is only one thing the proxy does to it: it replaces the token "__DATA__" with the JSON payload of your view.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Products</title>
<style>
/*__SHARED_CSS__*/
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div id="app"></div>
<script>
const PAYLOAD = "__DATA__";
 
function render(payload) {
  var items = (payload && payload.data.products && payload.data.products.value) || [];
  var app = document.getElementById('app');
 
  var h1 = document.createElement('h1');
  h1.textContent = items.length + ' products';
  app.appendChild(h1);
 
  var table = document.createElement('table');
  items.forEach(function (p) {
    var tr = document.createElement('tr');
    [p.Id, p.Name, p.Price].forEach(function (v) {
      var td = document.createElement('td');
      td.textContent = v == null ? '' : String(v);
      tr.appendChild(td);
    });
    table.appendChild(tr);
  });
  app.appendChild(table);
 
  /* let the host resize the iframe to the content */
  window.parent.postMessage({
    type: 'ui-size-change',
    payload: { height: document.documentElement.scrollHeight + 2 }
  }, '*');
}
 
/* The token is only an object once the proxy injected the payload. It is null
   in the data-less ui:// template variant and the literal string when you open
   this file straight from disk. */
render(typeof PAYLOAD === 'object' ? PAYLOAD : null);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Two things about this file.

The "__DATA__" token is quoted on purpose. This keeps the raw template valid JavaScript, so you can open the file directly in your browser while you are building it (you'll just get the literal string instead of data). Once the proxy renders it, the quoted token is replaced by the JSON object and PAYLOAD becomes:

{
  "view": "UI_ProductsOverview",
  "params": {},
  "data": { "products": { "value": [ ... ] } }
}

So your named data sources sit under data, exactly as the API returned them. Aggregating, grouping and sorting is your job here in the browser, the proxy does not reshape anything.

The second thing: use textContent, not innerHTML. Your data comes from a backend and ends up in a page. The proxy escapes < as \u003c in the injected JSON so a value can never close the script tag, but everything after that is your own responsibility.

Step 3: Declare the view in your config

Add a top-level ui array to api-config.json, next to apis:

{
  "server": { "name": "my-mcp-server", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "My custom MCP server" },
  "apis": [ ... ],
  "ui": [
    {
      "tool": "UI_ProductsOverview",
      "description": "Show an interactive table of all products. Prefer this over Products_list when the user wants to *see* the products.",
      "uri": "ui://my-mcp-server/products-overview",
      "template": "ui/products-overview.html",
      "data": {
        "products": { "api": "my-api", "path": "Products" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Field by field:

  • tool: the MCP tool name. I prefix all of mine with UI_ so they are easy to recognize in the tool list.
  • description: the tool description the model reads. This is the most important field of the whole entry, it decides whether the model picks your view or the plain data tool. Write it for the model, not for a human and say explicitly when it should be preferred.
  • uri: the ui:// resource URI. The template is also registered as an MCP resource on this URI, for hosts that pre-fetch templates.
  • template: path to your HTML file, relative to the config file.
  • data: your named data sources. api refers to the name of one of your APIs and path is relative to that API's pathPrefix.

Note that the request goes through the same OData client, the same destination and the same JWT as the generated Products_list tool. You are not opening a second door into your backend.

Step 4: Run it

Start the server as usual:

npm start

The log tells you the views were picked up:

UI registration complete: 1 view(s) registered

Small thing to know: the views are registered per MCP session, not once at boot. In stdio mode you see that line right at startup, with the default HTTP transport it appears the moment a client connects and again for every new session.

To test if it works I used the MCP Inspector. The default transport is HTTP on port 4004, so the server is reachable on http://localhost:4004/mcp:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

This opens the inspector in your browser. Connect it to http://localhost:4004/mcp, list the tools and call UI_ProductsOverview. In the tool result you should see three things: a short text summary, the ui://my-mcp-server/products-overview resource with the rendered HTML and the payload as structuredContent.

Once that works, connect it to Claude Desktop with MCP_TRANSPORT=stdio and ask "show me my products". The view is rendered right in the conversation.

If a data source fails, the tool result comes back as an error with the message of the failing request. That is what you want during development, but for a source that is only nice to have you can soften it:

"categories": { "api": "my-api", "path": "Categories", "optional": true }

With optional: true a failing source becomes null in the payload instead of failing the whole view.

Step 5: Add a parameter

A view without parameters always shows everything. To filter, add an inputs block. Every input is compiled into the tool's input schema, so the model knows it exists and the value is validated before your path is built:

{
  "tool": "UI_ProductsOverview",
  "description": "Show an interactive table of products, optionally filtered by category.",
  "uri": "ui://my-mcp-server/products-overview",
  "template": "ui/products-overview.html",
  "inputs": {
    "category": {
      "type": "string",
      "required": true,
      "description": "Category name to filter the products on"
    }
  },
  "data": {
    "products": { "api": "my-api", "path": "Products?$filter=Category eq '{category}'" }
  }
}

{category} is replaced with the validated argument, URL-encoded. Inputs can be string, number or boolean and instead of required you can give a default, which is applied while parsing so your placeholder always resolves. Number inputs also take min and max:

"months": { "type": "number", "default": 6, "min": 1, "max": 24, "description": "Reporting window in months" }

Next to your own parameters there is a small set of built-ins for dates and paging, which you'll need sooner than you think for anything reporting-like:

"usage": { "api": "my-api", "path": "Usage?from={$monthsAgo(months-1):yyyymm}&to={$now:yyyymm}" }
  • {$now:FMT}: the current UTC time
  • {$monthsAgo(N):FMT}: the first of the month, N months back
  • {$daysAgo(N):FMT}: N days back
  • FMT: yyyymm, date or iso

The months-1 is not a general expression, it is the only arithmetic that exists. It's there because a window of "the last 6 months including this one" cannot be written without it.

Step 6: Share the styling between views

Once you have a second view you don't want to copy your CSS into it. This can be done with partials, a plain map of a literal token to a file. Every occurrence of the token is replaced with the content of the file, before the data is injected.

Create ui/_shared.css:

body { font: 14px/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 0; padding: 16px; }
table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; }
td { border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 6px 8px; }

And point the token in your template at it:

"partials": {
  "/*__SHARED_CSS__*/": "ui/_shared.css"
}

The token in the template is /*__SHARED_CSS__*/, which is a comment in both CSS and JavaScript. So the template stays openable in the browser even before the proxy touches it.

Watch out here: every file you list is read from disk on the tool call, a partial pointing at a file that doesn't exist makes the whole view return an error. So only add an entry once the file is there. In my BTP MCP server I use the same trick for shared helper functions and even for the SVG path of the world map, which is way too long to keep inside the HTML.

Step 7: Navigate from one view to another

A view can ask the host to call another tool. This is a postMessage to the parent window:

function uiTool(toolName, params) {
  window.parent.postMessage({
    type: 'tool',
    messageId: 'ui-' + Date.now(),
    payload: { toolName: toolName, params: params || {} }
  }, '*');
}

Which you then hang on a button or a table row:

button.addEventListener('click', function () {
  uiTool('UI_ProductDetails', { productId: p.Id });
});

The host calls UI_ProductDetails with that parameter and renders the next view. This is how the drill-down in my BTP dashboards works: the overview navigates to the map, the map navigates back and a row navigates to the details of one subaccount.

Put this helper in a ui/_shared.js file, you'll use it in every view. Add the token to your template:

<script>
/*__SHARED_JS__*/
</script>

And the file to your partials, next to the CSS one:

"partials": {
  "/*__SHARED_CSS__*/": "ui/_shared.css",
  "/*__SHARED_JS__*/": "ui/_shared.js"
}

One more thing: render-data hosts

The template is also registered as a resource on its ui:// URI, with null instead of the payload. MCP Apps hosts can fetch that once and then send the data per tool call as a ui-lifecycle-iframe-render-data message, instead of rendering the page with the data baked in. The typeof PAYLOAD === 'object' guard from Step 2 keeps that case from crashing, but the view then shows an empty table until the message arrives.

If you want to support both delivery styles, listen for the message and render whichever data comes in first:

window.addEventListener('message', function (ev) {
  var m = ev.data;
  if (!m || m.type !== 'ui-lifecycle-iframe-render-data') return;
  var out = m.payload && m.payload.renderData && m.payload.renderData.toolOutput;
  var data = out && out.view ? out : (out && out.structuredContent) || null;
  if (data) render(data);
});

I have this in my _shared.js together with a guard so the view renders only once. Have a look at bootView in the BTP MCP server if you want the complete version.

Tip: develop the template outside the server

Restarting the MCP server for every CSS change gets old fast. Because the template is a plain HTML file with a quoted token, you can develop it standalone: copy the file, replace "__DATA__" with a fixture payload you captured from a real tool call and open it in your browser. Everything except the data fetching behaves identically.

I keep a small script for that. Nothing fancy, but it saved me a lot of restarts 🙂

Result

Your project now looks like this:

my-mcp-server/
├── package.json
├── api-config.json
├── .env
└── ui/
    ├── _shared.css
    ├── _shared.js
    └── products-overview.html

Still no application code. One config file, some HTML and you have an MCP server that answers with a UI instead of a paragraph.

A products table is where you start, it is not where you have to stop. This is the same mechanism applied to my BTP MCP server, an overview of all my subaccounts with stat tiles, a per-region chart and a searchable table:

The UI_SubaccountsOverview view rendered in the chat

The buttons in the header are the uiTool navigation of Step 7. Clicking "Locations map" makes the host call the geomap tool, which plots where all those subaccounts actually run:

The UI_GeomapDashboard view, reached by clicking "Locations map"

Five views, all declared the way you just declared one.

For the complete example with cross-navigation, a world map, pagination and a consumption dashboard, have a look at that repository. There is nothing in it except the config and the templates, so it is easy to copy from: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server

The full BTP OData MCP Proxy is here: https://github.com/lemaiwo/odata-mcp-proxy and can be used as a plugin from npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/odata-mcp-proxy

Conclusion

Adding a UI view to your MCP server is a template plus a config entry. The proxy handles the fetching, the parameter validation and the mcp-ui packaging, you handle the page. Start with a table, add a parameter when you need it and share the styling once you have a second view.

Contributions and feedback are welcome, the proxy is on GitHub and npm.

Kr, Wouter

entry.title: Practical AI in SAP Business One: from business questions to better decisions
entry.content:
For many SMEs, the most valuable AI opportunities are also the most practical: finding answers faster, reducing repetitive work and making better decisions.

The challenge is turning that potential into something genuinely useful.

AI can generate responses quickly. But business decisions rarely depend on a single piece of information or a simple answer. They depend on context – understanding the situation behind the question.

Why did sales drop?
Which customers need attention?
What’s affecting profitability?
How could a change in regulations impact operations?

The usefulness of AI depends on whether it can understand the business context behind those questions.

SAP Business One brings together the data and processes businesses rely on every day. By connecting AI with that context, SAP Business One creates new ways for people to explore their business – from asking questions more intuitively, to understanding what’s happening, to applying AI in more specialised scenarios.

Helping people find answers more naturally

Every business has questions. The challenge is often getting from the question to the answer.

Traditionally, exploring business data could require knowing which report to run, understanding how information is structured or asking someone with technical knowledge to create a database query.

That creates a gap between the people who understand the business question and the tools needed to answer it.

AI User Defined Query in SAP Business One helps close that gap.

Instead of writing a database query, users can describe the question they want to answer using everyday business language. AI User Defined Query tool, powered by SAP AI Core Services, generates the SQL script needed to retrieve the relevant data, which users can review before running it.

The process brings together the strengths of AI and human judgement: AI helps create the query, while users remain in control of reviewing the request and the results. At no point does AI directly access company data which is entirely secure.

But the real value is what happens next.

The results open in List View, where users can filter, sort and analyse the information further. Instead of producing another static report that answers one question and ends there, the results become a starting point for investigation.

A question leads to another question. A pattern leads to a deeper investigation.  If desired the List View can then be saved for future investigations.

The people closest to the business can explore what’s happening themselves, without needing to rely on someone else to prepare the answer.

 

From understanding what happened to exploring why

Business data tells a business what’s happening.

But many decisions require a wider perspective.

A change in regulations could affect operations. A shift in market conditions could influence demand. A supplier issue could require understanding factors beyond your own transactions.

Many AI experiences start with a blank prompt. Before AI can help, users need to explain the situation, provide the background and describe what they are trying to understand.

Ask AI in SAP Business One takes a secure approach, powered by the same SAP AI Core Services that supports AI User Defined Query

Using Ask AI, users can bring selected SAP Business One context into their question, combining business information from within SAP Business One with AI-based internet research. The user controls which field values and context are shared, while AI uses that context to provide a more relevant response. At no point does the AI gain direct access to the company database, and it knows only the specific data shared within the context of the question asked. 

The difference is subtle but important. Instead of asking a general question and then explaining why it matters, users can start with the business situation they are already exploring.

That makes AI usage secure and more useful for questions where internal business data is only part of the answer.

 

From everyday improvements to specialist capabilities

The most useful AI applications will look different for every business.

Some use cases will be straightforward: automating repetitive work, reducing manual steps or improving consistency in processes where accuracy matters.

Others will be more niche: capabilities designed around particular industries, roles or business scenarios.

That’s why SAP Business One is designed to support both built-in AI capabilities and further innovation through SAP and partner solutions.

SAP AI services can support scenarios such as document processing and automation, while SAP Business One extensibility enables partners to build additional AI solutions using SAP technologies. See the AI Partner Innovations Playbook for SAP Business One.

This creates a broader ecosystem where businesses can apply AI in the areas that matter most to them – whether that’s a common business need or a specialist capability for a particular market.

Making AI work for the people who know the business best

AI doesn’t replace the institutional knowledge that exists within a business.

The people closest to customers, suppliers, products and operations are often the ones asking the most salient questions. The opportunity is to give them better ways to explore those questions, understand what’s happening and act on what they discover.

SAP Business One brings AI closer to those everyday decisions.

By connecting AI with business context, it helps businesses move from simply having access to AI to using AI in ways that are practical, relevant and valuable.

For businesses, that means more opportunities to use AI not as a separate technology, but as part of how they understand their operations, respond to change and pursue new opportunities.

See It in Action

Watch Introducing New AI Capabilities in SAP Business One to see AI User Defined Query and Ask AI in action — and discover how these capabilities can help your business move from questions to decisions, faster.

▶ Watch the video

Ready to Explore What's Possible?

The AI capabilities described in this post are available in SAP Business One today. Whether you're an existing customer or exploring ERP for the first time, there are straightforward ways to take the next step.

Looking for a partner? SAP's global ecosystem of accredited partners provides consulting, implementation and support services to help you get up and running quickly. Find a partner →

Already running SAP Business One? Connect with your partner or access technical resources and product support experts via the SAP Support Portal.
