entry.title: OData MCP Proxy - Combining skills with MCP servers
entry.content:
Introduction

In my previous blog post I showed how the odata-mcp-proxy can turn an HTML page into an interactive MCP tool: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/odata-mcp-proxy-interactive-ui-views-in-your-mcp-server/ba-p/14469713

That post was about what comes out of the MCP server. This one is about what goes in: how does the model know which tool to call, what payload to send and how to keep the responses small?

What if the MCP server would only take care of the connection to the data source and something else would explain to the model how that server should be used? That something else exists, it is called a skill. A skill is a markdown file with instructions that the AI client loads when it needs it. The MCP server owns the connection, the skill owns the knowledge. Two different things, two different owners, two different places.

In this blog post, I'll walk you through how I combined a skill with my BTP MCP server, why this split improves performance, reduces token consumption and applies a kind of segregation of duty between the connection and the know-how. The full example is the btp-mcp-server project on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server

Problem

The btp-mcp-server exposes the BTP Core Services APIs (Accounts, Entitlements, Provisioning), the Usage Data Management API and the XSUAA SCIM and Authorization APIs as MCP tools. There is no application code in the project, the whole server is one config file for the odata-mcp-proxy and a folder with HTML views.

Exposing the APIs as tools is the easy part. The hard part is that the BTP APIs have a lot of small rules that the model can't guess from a JSON schema:

  • Entitling a service plan is an update on the Assignments entity set, not a create. And it is a collection-level update, so no key in the path.
  • A numeric quota uses "amount", a boolean plan uses "enable", sending both fails.
  • A Cloud Foundry org is an environment instance, not a subaccount.
  • Subaccounts use a region (eu10), environment instances use a landscapeLabel (cf-eu10).
  • The SCIM Users API takes ?filter=...&startIndex=...&count=..., not $filter and $top.
  • Every write is asynchronous, the response comes back before the work is done.

Without this knowledge the model makes a wrong call, reads the error, tries again, reads the next error and so on. Every attempt costs tokens and time and the user is watching the model struggle with the BTP API instead of getting an answer.

Next to that, the BTP list responses are verbose. An unfiltered list of assignments or subaccounts easily returns thousands of tokens of fields nobody asked for. The model needs to be told to use $select, $filter and $top, it doesn't do that by itself.

First fix: everything in the tool descriptions

My first fix was to enrich the descriptions of the entity sets in the config file. That is what every MCP client sees, so it seemed like the right place:

{
  "entitySet": "Assignments",
  "urlPath": "assignments",
  "description": "service plan entitlement assignments; use update to entitle or revoke plans for a subaccount (async); scope list to one subaccount",
  "category": "entitlements",
  "keys": [],
  "operations": { "list": true, "get": false, "create": false, "update": true, "delete": false }
}

This helps and I kept it, the hints in the descriptions benefit every MCP client. But a tool description is the wrong place for a payload example, a multi-step workflow or a list of pitfalls. Two reasons:

  1. Every character in a tool description is loaded into the context of every conversation, whether the user is going to entitle a service plan or not. With 40 tools that adds up fast.
  2. The description belongs to the server. The knowledge about how to use the server for a task belongs to whoever uses it. A BTP admin at one customer has different workflows and different rules than a BTP admin at another customer, the server is the same.

So I needed a place for the knowledge that is loaded only when needed and that lives next to the consumer instead of inside the server.

Solution

That place is a skill. In the btp-mcp-server repository there is a file .claude/skills/btp-admin/SKILL.md. It is a plain markdown file with a small frontmatter on top:

---
name: btp-admin
description: Administer SAP BTP through the btp-mcp-server MCP tools (subaccounts, directories, entitlements, environment instances, XSUAA role collections and roles) and visualize the landscape with the interactive UI_* dashboard tools. Use whenever the user asks to create, list, update, entitle, delete, or visualize anything in their BTP global account, e.g. "create a subaccount", "entitle a service", "show my subaccounts", "consumption dashboard", "where do my subaccounts run". Explains which tool to pick, required payloads, and how to keep responses small.
---

Only the name and the description are loaded when a conversation starts, that is a few dozen tokens. The moment the user asks something that matches the description ("entitle hana-cloud to my dev subaccount"), the full skill is loaded and the model has the complete manual for the server in front of it. When the user asks something unrelated, the manual stays closed. This is called progressive disclosure and it is the main reason a skill is cheaper than a tool description.

If you know the SAP world, an analogy: the MCP server is the OData service and the skill is the annotation file. The service gives you the entities and the operations, the annotations tell the consumer how to use them properly. You don't put the UI annotations inside the service implementation, you put them next to it.

What the MCP server does

The server does exactly one thing: it connects the AI client to the BTP APIs. This means:

  • The BTP destinations with the OAuth2 client credentials for each API
  • The XSUAA configuration with the MCPViewer, MCPEditor and MCPAdmin roles
  • Which entity sets and operations are exposed at all (Assignments has no create, GlobalAccount has no get)
  • The JSON schema of every tool

This is the part that needs to be deployed, secured and maintained by the platform team. It runs on BTP Cloud Foundry, it is bound to XSUAA and the Destination service and a user who doesn't have the write scope can't call an update, no matter what the model or the skill says.

What the skill does

The skill knows nothing about destinations or OAuth. It explains how to use the server for a task. The core of it is a task map:

Task

api

entitySet

operations

Global account details / GUID

cis-accounts

GlobalAccount

list

See or change service entitlements

cis-entitlements

Assignments

list, update

Cloud Foundry orgs / Kyma runtimes

cis-provisioning

EnvironmentInstances

list, get, create, delete

Monthly usage / consumption

uas-reporting

MonthlyUsage

list

Subaccount users (SCIM)

xsuaa-scim

Users

list, get

Role collections

xsuaa-authorization

RoleCollections

list, get, create, update, delete

 

Followed by the payload shapes the JSON schema can't express. This is the one for entitling a service plan:

{
  "subaccountServicePlans": [
    {
      "serviceName": "hana-cloud",
      "servicePlanName": "hana",
      "assignmentInfo": [
        { "subaccountGUID": "<guid>", "amount": 1 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

With the rules underneath:

  • Numeric-quota plans use "amount": <n> (set 0 to revoke).
  • Boolean plans use "enable": true / false instead of "amount", the two are mutually exclusive.
  • The call is asynchronous, verify with a scoped Assignments list afterwards.

Then the token discipline section, which is basically "on every list call: $select only what you need, $filter server-side, $top when exploring and fetch the GlobalAccount at most once per conversation". Then the multi-step workflows (onboard a subaccount with a Cloud Foundry org: create, entitle, pick a landscape, create the environment instance, poll until OK) and finally the pitfalls.

Nothing in that file can give the model access it doesn't have. It can only make the model use the access it has more efficiently.

Segregation of duty

This is the part I like most about the setup. Once the connection and the knowledge are split, they can be owned by different people:

 

MCP server

Skill

What

Connection to the data source

How to use that connection for a task

Contains

Destinations, XSUAA roles, exposed entity sets, schemas

Tool selection, payload shapes, workflows, pitfalls, token rules

Owner

Platform / integration team

The team or person using the server

Lives

Deployed on BTP

A markdown file in the consumer's repo or project

Changes when

An API or a destination changes

A process or a preference changes

Enforces

Authorization

Nothing, it only guides

 

A customer can write its own skill on top of the same server with its own naming conventions ("subdomains always start with the cost center"), its own approval rules ("never delete a subaccount, always ask") and its own workflows. The server doesn't change. The platform team doesn't need to redeploy anything when the BTP admin team decides that every new subaccount needs a specific label. And the other way around, when I ship a new version of the server with an extra API, the skill of the customer keeps working, it just doesn't know about the new API yet.

Compare that with putting everything in the tool descriptions: every process change becomes a config change and a redeployment of the server, by the team that owns the server.

Performance and token consumption

The skill was not the only thing I changed. Since version 1.3.0 the odata-mcp-proxy supports progressive tool discovery, which is a config switch:

"discovery": {
  "mode": "hybrid",
  "alwaysRegister": ["Subaccounts"],
  "maxResults": 25,
  "maxFullResults": 5
}

Before this, every operation of every entity set was its own tool. That was 40 tools and around 8,600 tokens of tools/list in every conversation before the user had typed anything. With hybrid mode only the pinned entity set (Subaccounts) keeps its five direct tools, everything else is reachable through two meta-tools: search_operations to find the right api, entity set and operation and execute_operation to run it.

 

Tools

tools/list

One tool per operation (before)

40

~8,600 tokens

hybrid, Subaccounts pinned (now)

12

~2,610 tokens

search mode, nothing pinned

7

~1,441 tokens

 

Now here is where the skill and the discovery mode reinforce each other. Discovery on its own adds a round trip: the model first has to call search_operations to find out that entitlements live in cis-entitlements / Assignments, only then it can call execute_operation. The task map in the skill already contains the api and entity set for every task. So in the common case the model skips the search completely and goes straight to execute_operation:

{
  "api": "cis-entitlements",
  "entitySet": "Assignments",
  "operation": "update",
  "body": { "subaccountServicePlans": [ ... ] }
}

Without the skill: small tool list, but an extra call for every task. Without discovery: no extra call, but 8,600 tokens of tool list in every conversation. With both: small tool list and no extra call, plus the payload is right the first time. That is what I mean with better performance: fewer calls, fewer failed calls and fewer retries.

How to use it

If you use Claude Code, cloning the repository is enough, the skill in .claude/skills/btp-admin/ is picked up automatically. The same works when you add the repository as a project in claude.ai. For other clients the SKILL.md is a plain markdown file, so it can be used as a system prompt or project instruction as well, you only lose the lazy loading.

The deployment of the server itself and the destinations it needs are described in the README of the project: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server

Conclusion

An MCP server should connect, a skill should explain. The server carries the destinations, the authorizations and the schemas and it is deployed once by the platform team. The skill carries the task map, the payload shapes, the workflows and the token rules and it lives with whoever uses the server. Split like that, the tool list stays small, the model skips the discovery round trip in most cases and the process knowledge can change without touching the server.

The segregation of duty is not a security feature by itself, the XSUAA roles on the server do that. It is a maintenance feature: two artifacts, two owners, two lifecycles.

Links

  • btp-mcp-server on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server
  • The btp-admin skill: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-mcp-server/blob/main/.claude/skills/btp-admin/SKILL.md
  • odata-mcp-proxy on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/odata-mcp-proxy
  • odata-mcp-proxy on npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/odata-mcp-proxy
  • Claude Code skills documentation: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
  • Previous post, interactive UI views: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/odata-mcp-proxy-interactive-ui-views-in-your-mcp-server/ba-p/14469713
  • Previous post, adding a UI view to your own MCP server: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/odata-mcp-proxy-how-to-add-a-ui-view-to-your-own-mcp-server/ba-p/14469719
  • First post, build your own SAP MCP server in minutes: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/build-your-own-sap-mcp-server-in-minutes-with-odata-mcp-proxy/ba-p/14348685

entry.title: Your ABAP backlog is not a capacity problem. We gave the AI toolchain to consultants, not developers
entry.content:
Two weeks later, for the first time in the company's history, we did not have enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue.

For years we had the same problem every SAP shop has. Not enough ABAP capacity. A queue of business requirements that never got shorter. Recruitment that never quite closed the gap, because senior ABAP people are scarce and expensive, and because the mid-level people you can actually hire need supervision from the senior people you could not hire.

We worked on this for a long time, and we worked on it hard. We tried a great deal, and for most of that time we treated it as a productivity problem, which is what everyone does. Make the developers faster. Give them better completion, better refactoring, better generation. Every one of those attempts produced something real, and none of them made the queue shorter.

Eventually we stopped and asked a different question: who is actually waiting?

The answer was not the developer. The developer was busy. The thing that was waiting was the requirement, and it was waiting in the gap between the person who understood it and the person who could implement it.

Reaching that conclusion took far longer than implementing it. Once we accepted it, we moved the tooling across that gap and gave it to the consultants.

That took two weeks. Nothing about our developers changed in those two weeks. Same people, same skills, same system. What changed was who started the work, and how much context survived before it started.

This article describes what we built, what it cost us to get there, what it does not do, and what we measured.

The bottleneck was never typing speed

Consider what happens to an ordinary custom requirement in an ordinary SAP project.

A business user describes what they need to a functional consultant. The consultant understands it, because the consultant sits close to the business and knows how this particular company has configured and extended SAP. The consultant writes it down. That document goes to a developer, who knows the system deeply but was not in the room and does not carry the business context. Meetings follow. The developer builds something. The consultant tests it, finds the three things the specification did not quite say, and explains again. Another round. Then another.

None of that is anybody's fault. It is a structural property of how the work is divided. Every hop across that boundary loses fidelity, and the loss is recovered through iteration, which is expensive and slow.

The second structural problem is testing. A developer often cannot meaningfully test what they built, because a real test needs business data, a business process and a judgement about whether the result is right. That judgement lives with the consultant. So the developer builds, hands over, waits, and then context-switches back days later to fix it.

Neither problem is solved by making the developer type faster. Both are solved by removing the hop.

What the rest of the industry is building right now

There is a lot of good work happening on AI-assisted ABAP development, and much of it is built on top of the development environment. Giving an AI assistant proper structured context about ABAP objects, instead of leaving it to infer from code completion, is a real improvement and the people doing it are doing it well.

We are not competing with that. We have a different goal, and one of our working principles is that we do not rebuild what the market already provides. Because everything here speaks MCP, those tools and ours can sit in the same landscape and serve the same consultant.

The difference is the audience. Tooling built on top of the development environment naturally serves the person who lives in the development environment. That improves the developer's part of the process. Our finding, after trying hard to improve exactly that part, is that the developer's part of the process was not the constraint.

The change we made

We built the toolchain for the consultant.

That is a different design problem. A consultant needs more than code generation. To take a requirement from a business user all the way to something testable, a consultant needs:

  • Knowledge of how this company has already built things, so the new thing is consistent with the old ones
  • Business data and transactions, so the result can be tested immediately against reality
  • Development tools, so the specification can become code
  • The company's own rules, so the code that comes out is the code this company would have written

Give a consultant those four things through an AI agent and something changes in the economics. The consultant does not translate the requirement to a developer. The consultant works the requirement into a functional specification, then a technical specification, then ABAP code, then tests it with real data, in one continuous session, while still holding the business context that made them the right person to understand it in the first place.

The magic is not the code generation. Code generation is a commodity. The magic is that a person who understands the requirement never has to hand it to someone who does not.

What the setup looks like

 Figure 1. The consultant works in one place. Four logical MCP servers supply knowledge, data, governance and tooling; the three platform-side ones can be deployed separately or combined. The interactive tier is exchangeable.

Four logical MCP servers, two backends, one place for the consultant to work. How they are deployed is a configuration choice, covered at the end of this section.

1. An MCP server published from the ABAP system itself

This is the piece that most differentiates the setup, so it is worth being precise about it.

The MCP server runs in the ABAP stack and is published through SICF. The reason is a different goal, not a different opinion about existing tooling. What this process needs from the ABAP system is business data, transactional actions and a handful of development tools, all provisioned under control. That is a provisioning problem, and the ABAP stack is where it gets solved.

None of that is a judgement about ADT. ADT is a development environment and it is very good at being one. This setup simply does not need that power to do its job, so we did not build toward it. If a customer wants it, the community MCP servers built on top of ADT connect alongside ours and serve the same consultant. We would far rather that happened than spend our time rebuilding something the market already provides and already does well.

Because it is published from the ABAP system, SAP's own authentication and authorization apply to every single call. There is no parallel permission model to maintain and no service user quietly holding more authority than the person using it. If a consultant is not authorized to see a plant, the agent does not see that plant either.

Provisioning is explicit and object by object. You nominate which tables, views and CDS views are exposed. You nominate which ABAP classes act as tools. There is a kill switch at the server.

Through it, the consultant's agent gets:

  • Business data: selected tables, views and CDS views
  • Business transactions: ABAP classes exposed as callable tools, so the agent can create and change documents the same way a user would
  • Development tools: read source code, read object metadata, read short dumps, inspect transports

That last group is what makes the specification honest. The agent does not recall what a table looks like. It reads it.

 Figure 2. The MCP server is a standard ICF service. Authentication and authorization are SAP's, not a parallel model.

 Figure 3. What the consultant actually sees: business transactions, nominated data sources and development tools in one list.

2. An MCP server for ABAP Code Intelligence

Most companies cannot answer a simple question about their own custom code: have we already built something like this?

Background AI agents on the Skybuffer AI platform read the entire custom estate out of the SAP backend and document it automatically. The documentation is vectorized immediately, which turns it into something the consultant's agent can search semantically during a task.

The effect is not mainly documentation for humans. It is that every new development starts with the question "what already exists here" answered. That raises integrity of the custom code base, drives reuse instead of reinvention, and surfaces harmonization and modernization candidates.

 Figure 4. Custom code is read, documented and vectorized continuously, so reuse is the default rather than an accident.

3. An MCP server for the company's development rules

Naming conventions. In-house ABAP standards. Clean ABAP. Clean core principles. Specification templates. The development contract that says what a functional specification must contain before it is allowed to become a technical specification.

These are usually in a wiki that nobody opens. Here they are in the task context, at the moment the decision is being made, which is the only moment they matter.

4. An MCP server for tooling

ABAP Cleaner and other post-processors, applied to generated code before a human looks at it.

This is deliberately an open ecosystem. SAP standard MCP servers, community ones, ADT-based servers for the developers who want them: they all connect alongside. Nothing here is exclusive, and nothing here duplicates something that already exists on the market.

A note on how these are deployed. The four above are a logical grouping rather than a required topology. The first is necessarily its own server, because it lives in the ABAP stack. The three provisioned from the Skybuffer AI platform can run as three servers or be combined into one, and which tools each exposes is configured per customer. We run ours combined, because our internal development process is a single process; a customer whose code standards and tooling sit with different owners may well want them apart. The configuration follows the customer's development process rather than the other way round.

 Figure 5. Platform-side tooling, here deployed as a single combined MCP server: search the documented estate, apply in-house rules, clean the generated code.

The orchestration layer

The MCP servers are the asset. The orchestration unit connects to them and can be exchanged. Which model sits there is a current engineering choice, and we cover the reasoning below.

Where the data lives, and who can support it

In serious conversations about this, two questions arrive before the technical ones. They deserve direct answers.

Your data stays yours, in your own infrastructure

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise. Either way it is the customer's landscape. The documented custom code, the vector store built from it, the in-house rule base and the configuration of the development process all sit inside the customer's infrastructure and belong to the customer.

The MCP server that exposes business data runs inside the ABAP stack itself. Data is not copied out to a platform so that an agent can reach it. It is read in place, per call, under the requesting user's own SAP authorizations. Nothing is staged, replicated or synchronised into a third-party store to make any of this work.

This is a consequence of the architecture rather than a policy bolted on top of it. There is no separate data layer to govern, because there is no separate copy of the data.

Built on SAP technologies, so anyone who supports SAP can support this

The solution is developed using SAP technologies only. It is an ABAP add-on plus a BTP or HANA application. It is not a black box with a proprietary runtime or a specialist skill set attached to it.

That has a consequence people tend to underestimate at purchase time and feel sharply two years later: your own internal SAP team can support it, and so can any SAP partner you already work with. You are not introducing a component into your landscape that only one vendor is able to touch, and you are not making your ABAP estate dependent on a skill set your team does not have and cannot hire.

No lock-in to a closed architecture

Nothing here requires a particular cloud offering. The platform deploys where you already run SAP. The MCP layer is an open protocol, which is why customers can add SAP standard or community MCP servers next to ours, and why the orchestration unit can be exchanged without rebuilding anything underneath it.

The thing you are investing in is your own documented custom estate, your own rule base and your own provisioned tool set. Those stay yours regardless of what you decide to run on top of them.

Two model tiers, chosen for two different jobs

There is no single "the AI" in this architecture. There are two tiers doing unrelated work, and they are not staffed by the same model for good reasons.

The background tier runs on the customer's own model, usually self-hosted. The agents that read the entire custom code estate, document it and vectorize it are doing bulk work where latency is not a KPI anyone is optimizing. If a full pass takes a weekend, nothing is harmed. That makes them a natural fit for a self-hosted LLM inside the customer's landscape, which is what most customers choose. Some run them on a single small GPU unit; an NVIDIA DGX Spark class device is enough for this workload.

This tier matters most for the data question, because this is the tier that touches everything. Every custom object, every piece of business logic, the complete estate. That entire pass happens inside the customer's infrastructure, on a model the customer selected, and the resulting knowledge base stays there.

The interactive tier is where the consultant works, and today we run Opus 5 Max there. That choice is specific rather than incidental, and the reason is not "it writes nice code."

The constraint is discipline under a governed process. Our development contract requires the agent to read the framework contract from live implementations rather than recall it, to verify every table and field against the live dictionary, and to stop when something cannot be verified. A model that shortcuts tool calls to produce a faster, more complete-looking answer breaks that contract no matter how good the templates are.

So what we need from the interactive model is narrower than general capability. It has to keep calling tools, as many times as the task actually requires, until the context is genuinely complete. And it has to hold and reason over the very large runtime context that results from doing so. As of today, that combination is what Opus 5 Max does well, and it is why the generated ABAP comes out integrated with the existing custom development and accurate to the customer's backend release rather than to a plausible average of the internet.

One honest boundary

The interactive tier is the single component that can sit outside the landscape. What crosses is the context assembled for one task, not the estate. We would rather state that plainly than let a reader discover it.

The architecture is built so that this position is exchangeable, which is the practical answer for anyone whose isolation requirements are absolute: point the interactive tier at a self-hosted model as well. Nothing underneath changes, because the MCP servers, the knowledge base and the governance do not care what is connected to them. The honest trade-off is that today you will give up some code quality by doing so, and how much depends on how well the model you choose sustains long tool-calling chains.

Why this does not just produce confident nonsense

This is the first question every experienced SAP person asks, and they are right to ask it.

The answer is not "the model is good." The answer is that the process forbids guessing, and the tooling makes not guessing cheaper than guessing.

A worked example from our own governed pipeline. The agent was building a new MCP tool and needed the framework contract: superclass, method signatures, error mechanism. The rule in our development contract is that it must read this from existing implementations, never recall it. So it read five objects in a fixed order.

Two things came out of that which no amount of model quality would have produced:

First, the metadata-reading tool reports a blank superclass for classes that genuinely do inherit. Reading the source instead showed the real inheritance. An agent working from metadata alone would have generated a structurally wrong class that implemented interfaces directly instead of inheriting from the framework base. It would have looked plausible and failed on activation.

Second, and more instructive: the specification needed two SAP authorization objects. The agent could not verify them. The system exposes no metadata path for authorization objects, and no existing tool in our library performed a comparable check that could be read as precedent. A generative tool optimizing for a complete-looking answer would have filled in the two most likely names.

It did not. It recorded them as unverified, raised a blocking open question with a named owner, isolated the two values in the code as single-point-of-change constants, and stated that the object must not be transported beyond development until a human confirms them.

That is the difference between a demo and a development process. The valuable output is not only the code. It is the code plus an explicit, honest list of what is still unknown.

What a task actually looks like

  1. The consultant brings a business requirement, usually straight from the conversation with the user.
  2. The agent loads the governed context: templates, in-house rules, and a semantic search of what already exists in the custom estate.
  3. Together they produce a functional specification. The agent verifies every table and field it names against the live system as it writes.
  4. The functional specification becomes a technical specification, with the framework contract read from real implementations rather than recalled.
  5. Code is generated from the technical specification, then run through ABAP Cleaner.
  6. The consultant tests it immediately, using the business transactions and data exposed through the same MCP server, without leaving the session or booking anyone's time.
  7. Unknowns that could not be resolved are listed as open questions with owners. Blocking ones stop the object from moving forward.

Steps 3 through 6 used to be a multi-week loop involving at least two people and several meetings.

What we measured

Inside our own company, within the first weeks:

  • About 40% reduction in the ABAP development capacity we needed. This is not a ceiling. We are still optimizing.
  • For the first time ever, not enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue — an inversion of the constraint we had been fighting for years.
  • Consultants completing volumes of work in one to two weeks that previously took far longer.

With a customer already running the new process, the effect showed up almost immediately. These are results from the first weeks of adoption, not from a mature steady state:

  • A backlog of critical business requirements cleared, after sitting unaddressed
  • Most projects delivered to UAT within one month
  • Up to 90% savings per project
  • $0.1M–$0.2M USD returned each week

The number the customer cared about most was none of those. It was that the queue of business requirements shrank. Business users stopped hearing "that is in the backlog" as the standard answer to a reasonable request.

That speed of return is the part worth pausing on. This is not a transformation programme that pays back over two years. The mechanism is simply that work stops waiting in a handoff, so the effect appears as soon as the first requirements go through the new path.

Set against the roughly 10% cost saving that classic developer-focused automation typically delivers, the difference is not incremental. It comes from moving the work, not from speeding up the typing.

The honest part

A few things we would want to know if we were reading this rather than writing it.

The consultant's job gets harder, not easier. This surprised us. Consultants were exhausted by the old cycle of meetings, explanation, testing and re-explanation, and they were glad to see it go. But spending the day in dialogue with a very knowledgeable agent is intense work. It demands more decisions per hour than the old process did. Our consultants report being happier, and they also report being more tired. Plan for that.

You still need ABAP developers. Complex architecture, performance work at scale, framework-level changes, and review of anything sensitive still need senior ABAP judgement. What changes is the ratio, and what those developers spend their day on. We reduced capacity by 40%; we did not reduce it to zero, and we would not want to.

This requires governance to exist before it can be automated. If your naming conventions, development standards and specification templates are informal or absent, the agent has nothing to be grounded in and you will get plausible, inconsistent output. The uncomfortable prerequisite is writing your rules down.

The first weeks are not representative. Early gains come partly from clearing a backlog that had accumulated. The steady-state number is lower than the first-month number. We are still measuring ours.

Where to start

You do not have to do all of this at once, and you should not.

  1. Make your custom estate legible. Run automated documentation over existing custom code and vectorize it. This has standalone value even if you stop here, because it answers "what do we already have" for every future project.
  2. Publish a narrow MCP server from your ABAP system. Start read-only, with a small set of nominated tables and development tools. SAP authorization does the access control, so the blast radius is whatever you provision.
  3. Write down the rules. Naming conventions, in-house standards, and one governed specification template. Put them where the agent reads them.
  4. Pick one consultant and one real requirement. Not a pilot with a toy scope. A real thing somebody is waiting for.
  5. Add transactional tools only once reading is solid, so the consultant can test in the same session.

Closing

We spent a long time, and a great deal of effort, trying to make developers faster before we accepted that we were optimizing the wrong side of the handoff. That conclusion was harder to reach than it looks written down, and we would not have believed it without running it on ourselves first.

The result is not that ABAP developers are unnecessary. It is that a large share of custom development does not need to cross the boundary between the person who understands the requirement and the person who implements it. When it does not have to cross, it does not have to wait.

If your business users are being told their requirements are in the queue, the queue is probably not a capacity problem. It is probably a translation problem.

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise, inside the customer's own landscape, and is built entirely on SAP technologies, so an internal SAP team or any SAP partner can support it. It is available on SAP Store. It was SAP Certified as Built with SAP Business AI, and was a finalist in the SAP Innovation Awards 2025 as a partner-built product. If you are working on the same problem from the developer side, we would like to compare notes, and we are genuinely interested in where this approach breaks.

entry.title: Agentic AI on BTP: Your Own Joule for Consultants, Connected to Your Own System
entry.content:
Introduction

What if you had something like Joule for Consultants, but connected to your own SAP system? Not just an assistant that knows the SAP documentation, but one that can also open the classes, CDS views and transports in the system you’re actually working on.

In my previous blog post, I introduced the dynamic multi-agent app: an orchestrator with specialist agents that are created, edited and reloaded at runtime, no redeploy needed: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-dynamic-multi-agent-on-demand-with-pydantic-ai/ba-p/14388032

That post ended with the claim that any MCP server can become a specialist agent with a row in a database. In this blog post, I’ll show you exactly how far that claim goes by configuring an ABAP agent that combines the SAP documentation MCP servers from @Marian_Zeis with ARC-1, an ADT MCP server that connects to a real ABAP system. The result behaves like a Joule for Consultants that knows your own landscape, purely by configuration.

Problem

Joule for Consultants is a nice idea: an AI assistant for SAP consultants with access to SAP knowledge, so you don’t have to dig through the Help Portal for every question. However, in practice it has two limitations that bother me.

First, it is not integrated into your own system. It can tell you how a CDS view works in general, but it has no idea which CDS views exist in your development system, how your Z-classes are built or what’s sitting in your open transport requests. As a consultant, that’s exactly the context you need, generic answers you can get from any chatbot.

Second, it comes with a cost per user. You pay per seat whether that consultant asks three questions a month or three hundred. For a small team that wants to experiment, that model is hard to justify.

Next to that, there is a bigger problem than Joule itself. Many companies simply don’t have a clear AI strategy yet, or they have Microsoft Copilot or something similar rolled out with not enough licenses to go around. And even when you do have such a license, it usually doesn’t allow you to connect your own MCP servers to it. So the SAP team ends up waiting for a company-wide decision that may take years.

This setup lets you get started on your own, within your SAP team, without waiting for that strategy. The only thing you need is BTP credits.

So what I actually want is:

  • Answers grounded in the official SAP documentation (ABAP keyword docs, SAP Help, RAP, CDS) instead of whatever the model remembers from training
  • Live access to my own ABAP system: search objects, read source code, run where-used analysis, check transports
  • The user’s own identity propagated to that system, so authorizations and audit still work
  • Pay for what you use (LLM tokens) instead of per user

Solution

The dynamic multi-agent app from the previous post already has everything needed for this, I just had to configure it. I created one new specialist agent, the ABAP Development Agent, and pointed it at three MCP servers:

  • The SAP Docs MCP server from Marian Zeis: SAP Help Portal, Discovery Center, released-object metadata and SAP Community content
  • ARC-1, also from Marian Zeis: a secure MCP proxy around the ADT REST API that connects to a real ABAP system

No custom code required. Just configuration. 🙂

The first server is publicly hosted, you can use them straight away without any setup. ARC-1 you deploy yourself, in my case as a Cloud Foundry app on BTP in front of my ABAP system.

To be clear, this doesn’t magically turn it into Joule. It won’t have SAP’s curated implementation content or learning journeys. Nevertheless, for the day-to-day questions a consultant or developer asks (“how does this statement work”, “where is this CDS view used”, “what’s in this class”), the combination of official docs plus your real system gets you surprisingly far.

What changed in the app: multiple MCP servers per agent

Since the previous post, the app supports connecting one agent to more than one MCP server. Each server is registered with its own auth mode:

Auth mode

When to use

How the user authenticates

jwt

BTP-hosted servers that trust this app’s XSUAA (HTTPS on *.hana.ondemand.com)

The user’s XSUAA JWT is forwarded on every request

oauth2

Servers with their own authorization server, like an ABAP system behind ARC-1

Per-user OAuth2 authorization_code, sign in once

none

Public servers that need no authentication

No token is sent

Next to that, there are a few more auth modes for the built-in toolsets: app-only client credentials, a BTP destination and a browser session you refresh by hand. For this scenario you only need the three above.

Registering an MCP server for an agent feels a lot like creating a destination in the BTP cockpit: you point at a URL, pick an auth type and you’re done.

The oauth2 mode is the interesting one for the ABAP scenario. The app supports Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591): tick “Dynamic registration”, fill in nothing else and on first use the app reads the MCP server’s OAuth metadata and registers itself as a client. The first time a user triggers the ABAP agent, the chat returns an Authorize link, the user signs in to the ABAP system once and from then on their own tokens are stored per user and forwarded on every call. This means the ABAP system sees the actual consultant, not a shared service account, per-user authorizations and audit are preserved.

In the meantime the app also got skills, workflows, scheduled job runs and a few built-in toolsets. You don’t need any of them for this scenario, so I’ll keep those for another post.

Configuring the ABAP agent

Everything happens in the admin UI. Since the previous post it got a SAPUI5 version, served at /ui5admin next to the original one at /admin. Both use the same backend and the same database, so it doesn’t matter which one you take, only the labels are a bit different. The screenshots below are from the UI5 admin.

  • Open /ui5admin and click “New agent” in the Agents list:

  • In the General panel, fill in the name, description and instructions for the specialist. The “Enabled” and “Available in chat” switches are on by default.
  • Next, add the servers in the Toolsets panel with the “Add toolset” button. For each one you fill in the URL and pick the auth mode, for ARC-1 you also tick “Dynamic registration”:

 

 

One thing to keep in mind here: by default only HTTPS URLs on *.hana.ondemand.com can be registered for the authenticated modes. Public servers on auth mode none are not restricted, so the two documentation servers work straight away. If your ARC-1 runs somewhere else, you need to put its URL in the MCP_URL_ALLOWLIST env var of the app.

  • Once saved, go to Settings and click “Reload” in the Lifecycle panel. This rebuilds the orchestrator in memory, the new specialist is available in the chat from the very next message. You can validate if this was successful by asking a question in the chat and checking that the steps of the new specialist show up in the answer.

Because agent definitions are just data, the whole thing can also be captured as a JSON snapshot with the Export and Import buttons in Settings. An export carries the orchestrator instructions, the skills, the agents and the workflows. Below is the agent part of it, which is also included as agents.seed.json in the repo:

{
  "version": 1,
  "orchestrator_instructions": "You are an orchestration agent for SAP development and operations tasks. You do not perform technical work directly, instead you interpret the user's intent and delegate to the appropriate specialist agent, then synthesize their output into a clear response. ...",
  "agents": [
    {
      "name": "ABAP Development Agent",
      "description": "Search and retrieve SAP product documentation: ABAP, SAPUI5, Fiori, CAP, BTP services, and general SAP developer docs. Use for reference lookups and how-to questions.",
      "instructions": "An autonomous ABAP development assistant that combines authoritative SAP documentation lookup with live system access via ARC-1. ...",
      "mcp_servers": [
        {
          "url": "http://mcp-sap-docs.marianzeis.de/mcp",
          "auth_mode": "none"
        },
        {
          "url": "https://<your-arc-1-deployment>/mcp",
          "auth_mode": "oauth2",
          "oauth": {
            "dcr": true,
            "has_client_secret": false
          }
        }
      ],
      "enabled": true
    }
  ]
}

The full instructions are in the repo, the short version: the agent is told it can ground answers in the ABAP/RAP documentation, read and navigate objects in the connected system via ADT, compute CDS blast-radius, run linting, diagnose dumps, query system tables and manage transports.

You could argue that one agent with three MCP servers gets a rather long tool list for a single specialist. So far it works fine, the servers expose focused tools (ARC-1 deliberately ships 12 intent-based tools instead of 200+ endpoint wrappers). Splitting documentation and system access into two specialists is always possible later, it’s just another row in the database.

The result

Once the agent is reloaded, the chat behaves like a consultant assistant. Asking “can you explain me how to create a cds view in an abap system?” makes the orchestrator delegate to the specialist, which grounds its answer in the ABAP documentation:

Next to that, questions like “show me the source of class ZCL_…” or “where is CDS view Z… used?” go through ARC-1 into the connected system, after the one-time Authorize step, with the user’s own credentials.

 

A word on safety: ARC-1 is read-only by default. Writes, data preview and free SQL each require explicit flags on the server and package allowlists restrict where anything can be created. For a consultant assistant, read-only is exactly what you want to start with.

Cost

There is no per-user license anywhere in this setup. The moving parts are the python app and its approuter on Cloud Foundry, a PostgreSQL instance, the HTML5 application repository for the UI5 admin, the ARC-1 deployment and the LLM consumption through SAP AI Core’s Generative AI Hub. You pay for tokens when people actually use it. Ten consultants who ask ten questions a day cost you their token usage, not ten seats.

Everything runs on BTP, so all of it is covered by your existing BTP contract. If you’re on a consumption-based model with credits left at the end of the contract year, this is a nice way to turn them into something your team actually benefits from instead of losing them.

Conclusion

The previous post promised that any MCP server can become a specialist agent with a row in a database. This post cashed in on that promise: by registering three existing MCP servers in the admin UI, the platform turned into an SAP assistant that knows both the official documentation and my own ABAP system, with the user’s identity flowing through on every call. In the end, the “own Joule for Consultants” was a configuration exercise, not a development project.

Contributions and feedback are welcome! The full source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app

entry.title: A closer look to the MCP Server of SAP BTP Integation Suite
entry.content:
1. What is the relationship among MCP Server, AI APP and Large Language Model(LLM)

MCP server is nothing but a special wrap up of SAP interfaces. It does NOT have any intelligence at all.

AI APP is a sort of software program, normally has a user friendly UI developed by python or Rust or C# or Typescript or Javascript etc. which ususally has a user interactive functionalily. The AI APP does NOT have any intelligence. It directly consumes MCP server's service, or it consumes services of LLM.

Large Language Model(LLM) is a component which has artificial intelligence. It can understand human natual language and output result inform of human natual language. Some examples of LLM are, OpenAI GPT series, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude etc.

In general, inside the AI APP, MCP server helps LLM deal with SAP data.

2. How to create a provider based API proxy in the Integration Suite.

Before the creation of MCP Server, a source API proxy in the CPI layer has to be created. This process has not been included in Ashutosh's tutorial. Let me add it here.

Let's take the OData v2 API Product as an example. (OData v4 is technically feasible. However its catelog service is not supported by the BTP API Management and it makes the process more complex.)

Version -4.12.6

Maybe this issue has been fixed by any versions afterwards, anyway in this version , by default the generated OData adapter doesn't support csrf-token. When try to change or create something via the API Proxy, we will get an error saying

before the step 'Request-Reply', add a content modifier.

insert a static http header as below

content-type: application/json; charset=iso-8859-1

now you can save the API proxy and deploy it.

create a MCP server by choosing the above API proxy

choose tools from the API Proxy resource list

then add this line to the resources

Save and deploy.

Now let's have few calls to the MCP server configured. Please be aware that for all calls to MCP server, the URL is the same as above. therefore i just paste the request payload

{

  "method": "tools/list",

the prompts maintain in MCP server to be used by two roles.

if the role is user, the prompt is to be used by AI APP, displaying some clue or hint to the real user. like for this example, product description update, 

step 1. user clicks a button on the AI APP to list all prompts.

step 2. AI APP list all user prompts in a user friendly way.

step 3. user chooses option 'update product description'

step 4. AI APP gets the prompt of 'update product description' and it displays a form including three mandatory fields:

language, new description and product id. This form should be generated based on the user prompt retrieved. 

step 5. AI APP collects what the user has inputted for these three fields. if anyone is missing, the AI APP can ask user provide before all information is ready.

step 6. AI APP sends the collected values of three fields together with the Assistant prompt to Large Language Model. The LLM should be able to consume the relevant MCP tool service to update the description.

source is used for relatively static URL for GET , or in the OData term, READ

if a GET call is based on dynamic condition, we put it in tools. in OData term, the QUERY is used here. This is an example payload

}

 

4.7 An example of UPDATE

{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "method": "tools/call",
    "id": 1,
    "params": {
        "name": "patch_A_ProductDescription_Product_Product_Language_Language",
        "arguments": {
            "Product": "422",
            "requestBody": {
                "d": {
                    "ProductDescription": "test by stephen"
                }
            },
            "Language": "EN"
        }
    }
}

 

5. Conclusion

  • MCP Server has no intelligence
  • MCP Server is a wrap up of exsiting system interfaces
  • The services of MCP server help system interfaces to be used by Large Language Model. This process is normally encapsulated inside an AI APP.

entry.title: Translating Regulatory Documents with BTP Translation Hub - A Use Case
entry.content:
I recently came across a use case I think is worth sharing with the community.

A customer running S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition had a localization challenge: regulatory PDF documents generated by the system were available in the local country language, with no English version. In this particular case, the customer, being a global company,  is using a shared corporate language across teams, so this was a real operational blocker.

The solution was already in SAP´s ecosystem,  SAP BTP Translation Hub.

SAP Translation Hub is an AI-powered translation service available on SAP BTP. It enables automated translation of text and documents using machine learning models, directly within the SAP ecosystem. The customer confirmed it worked for their needs and adopted it.

A solution for a common challenge

Any company running S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition across multiple countries may encounter the same friction:

  • Country-specific legal or tax documents (e-invoicing, eDocuments, statutory reports) available only in the local language
  • Multi-country rollouts where a shared corporate language is required
  • Scenarios where a standard product feature is on the roadmap but not yet delivered

In all of these, BTP Translation Hub can serve as a practical, low-effort bridge. The Document Translation capability specifically covers this kind of use case.

Key aspects to consider about the service

  • Licensing is character-based, so it scales with your actual usage, no heavy upfront commitment. You can review the commercial options on the SAP Discovery Center and the Enterprise and Free Tier account details on the Help Portal
  • It runs natively on BTP, so there's no need to integrate external translation tools
  • Setup is relatively lightweight ,  the Initial Setup guide on the Help Portal walks you through it, and SAP Developers also has a step-by-step tutorial if you prefer a hands-on approach

The full product documentation is available on the SAP Help Portal.

 

If you've faced similar localization challenges in your S/4HANA Cloud implementations, I'd be curious to hear how you've handled them and whether BTP Translation Hub has come up in your projects.

SAP JOULE

SAP Managed Joule | Provisioning and Testing Approaches

Purpose

This guide helps Line of Business (LOB) teams test Joule integration with their systems using the recommended customer-like end-to-end approach.

Testing Approach Selection

Option 1: Level 2 - Customer-like E2E Testing (Recommended)

Prerequisites:

  • The same IAS (Identity Authentication Service) must be used across the entire setup
  • Core components must be in place before running Joule Core

Why Level 2 is Recommended:

  • Complete customer-like end-to-end validation
  • All dependent formations are created automatically (Core Components, Joule Work)
  • Tests full SAP Managed Joule integration flow
  • Validates your LOB integration in a realistic customer environment
  • Ensures all cross-component dependencies work correctly

What You Get:

  • Full formation with core components
  • Joule Work Development environment (requires SKU: 8019544)
  • SAP Managed Joule (SMJ) integration
  • Your LOB system integration

When to Use:

entry.title: The Future of Global Treasury: Building Intelligent Payment Architecture with SAP S/4HANA
entry.content:
For years, enterprise payments were treated as the final step of a financial process — invoices approved, payment runs executed, files sent to banks, and transactions completed.

That model is changing.

Today, payments sit at the intersection of liquidity, connectivity, cybersecurity, compliance, and business continuity. The question is no longer “How do we send a payment file?” but “How do we build an intelligent, controlled, and globally scalable ecosystem where money moves securely and transparently?”

For organizations advancing toward SAP S/4HANA, this shift opens a powerful opportunity: to reimagine treasury not as a back‑office function but as the strategic intelligence center of the enterprise.

From Processing to Intelligence

Traditional payment landscapes often evolve into fragmented networks — multiple banks, diverse formats, inconsistent approvals. Technically functional, yes; operationally complex, absolutely.

The next generation of treasury must move beyond processing toward payment intelligence — a unified architecture built on four pillars:

 Visibility and Liquidity — The Strategic Core

Visibility tells us where the money is.

Visibility and Liquidity — The Strategic Core

Visibility tells us where the money is. Liquidity intelligence tells us what to do with it.

SAP S/4HANA brings together transactions, statements, and payment data into a single digital foundation. When paired with intelligent forecasting and automation, treasury shifts from reacting to events to anticipating them — transforming cash management into a predictive discipline.

Technology doesn’t replace judgment; it amplifies it.

 

Connectivity and Standardization

For global enterprises, bank integration is rarely simple. Multiple regions, formats, and regulations demand a deliberate connectivity strategy.

SAP’s Bank Communication Management and Multi‑Bank Connectivity enable scalable, secure integration — but architecture must come before technology.

This is where ISO 20022 becomes transformative. Beyond compliance, its structured data model enhances automation, reconciliation, and transparency across the payment lifecycle. Organizations that treat ISO 20022 as a mere deadline risk missing its strategic potential.

 

Workflow, Controls, and Trust

Speed without control is risk.

Effective payment governance defines who can move money and under what conditions. Approval thresholds, dual control, exception handling, and auditability must be embedded into architecture — not bolted on later.

The goal: exception‑driven treasury. Routine transactions flow seamlessly; human attention focuses only where intervention truly matters.

 

The Emerging Role of AI

AI is reshaping treasury from reactive operations to proactive intelligence.

Imagine systems that not only flag failed payments but diagnose causes and route resolutions. Forecasting models that learn from patterns to refine liquidity predictions.

Yet intelligence must always be governed. In finance, control is the foundation of trust. The future isn’t AI replacing professionals — it’s professionals empowered by intelligent systems.

 

Architecture Before Technology

Technology alone doesn’t create transformation. Architecture does.

Define operating principles first:

  • What should be global vs. local?

  • Where should approvals occur?

  • Who owns connectivity?

  • How are exceptions managed?

Once these are clear, technology becomes an enabler, not a substitute.

 

Treasury as a Strategic Intelligence Function

Modern treasury is evolving from transaction execution to enterprise insight.

It helps organizations understand not only where money is, but why it moves, what could interrupt it, and how capital can be deployed more effectively.

That is the essence of FLOW — where visibility informs liquidity, liquidity informs payments, and payments operate through optimized connectivity, all protected by intelligent workflow and controls.

When an organization can truly understand and manage the flow of its money, treasury stops being the function that moves cash. It becomes the function that decides how money should move next.

entry.title: Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent?
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

A customer may have a governed purchase order data product and ask whether it can be used to build an agent. My answer would be to look first at what the agent is expected to do. Imagine an agent helping a procurement team with delayed orders. A user asks why an order is late and what should happen next.

 

Figure: The five readiness checks for a purchase order data product.

Five checks before the agent uses it

First, define the business meaning. Does late refer to the original delivery date or the latest confirmed date? Is a partially delivered item late? Which status is authoritative? These questions sound basic until an agent has to explain an exception without a buyer beside it.

Second, map the context. The answer may depend on the supplier, contract, goods receipt and current delivery commitment. If that commitment is in an inaccessible email, the agent should say its information is incomplete.

Third, check trust. When were the records updated? Are the fields complete? Can we trace the figures to their source? An unposted goods receipt can make the order look late even when the goods have arrived.

Fourth, test access end to end. A buyer may see only orders within a purchasing organization. The agent’s data access and every tool call must respect the relevant scope. SAP Datasphere data access controls can help restrict rows in protected objects, but the complete path still needs to be tested.

Fifth, define the action. Explaining a delay, recommending a supplier call, creating a task and changing a purchase order have different consequences. The right to read an order is not the right to change it.

A useful starting outcome

I would start with an agent that explains the exception, shows its evidence and points out missing information. Procurement users can then assess whether the result is dependable. Once that works, the business can define which follow-up actions are appropriate and where approval belongs.

The architecture question is not simply whether a data product exists. It is whether the data product and its surrounding context are fit for the exact decision and level of autonomy we expect.

For the purchase order pilot, I would ask the buyer to walk through two real exceptions. One should have complete records; the other should include a missing or conflicting commitment. Those cases show whether the agent can explain uncertainty rather than turn an incomplete picture into a confident instruction.

The same review should include the user experience. If an agent lacks the contract, it should tell the buyer what it checked and suggest who can confirm the commitment. That response is still useful. It respects the limit of the available information and helps the person complete the work.
