entry.title: Using SAP Integration Suite AI Adapter to turn integration failures into actionable insights
entry.content:
Using SAP Integration Suite AI Adapter to turn integration failures into actionable insights

Introduction

Integration monitoring is an essential part of every integration landscape.

When customers have hundreds or even thousands of integrations running every day, monitoring becomes critical to identifying failed messages, understanding what happened, and taking corrective actions.

But there is an important question that goes beyond simply detecting a failure:

When an integration fails, how quickly can we understand what happened and what we should do next?

In many integration scenarios, the monitoring platform tells us that something went wrong. The next step still requires a person to open the Message Processing Log (MPL), analyze the failed step, inspect the backend response, and determine the probable root cause.

This is where I see an interesting opportunity for AI.

Instead of using AI to replace integration monitoring, we can use it to add an intelligence layer on top of the monitoring process.

In this blog, I will show a Proof of Concept using SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration, SAP Generative AI Hub, and the AI Adapter, where an integration failure automatically triggers an AI-based analysis that can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

The Challenge: An Integration Error Is Often Just the Beginning

Imagine that an integration fails and the monitoring team receives:

 

 
HTTP 400 - Bad Request
Technically, this is useful information. However, from an operational perspective, the investigation has just started.

The support analyst may need to:

  1. Open the Message Processing Log.
  2. Identify the failed step.
  3. Inspect the backend response.
  4. Understand which business process was being executed.
  5. Identify the probable root cause.
  6. Determine the business impact.
  7. Decide whether the message can be safely reprocessed.

    When this happens occasionally, this process is manageable.

    When it happens hundreds of times across a large integration landscape, the amount of manual analysis can become significant.

    This led me to explore a simple question:

    What if AI could perform the first level of incident analysis when an integration fails?

    The Concept

    The idea is not to replace the Message Processing Log or the existing integration monitoring capabilities.

    Instead, the architecture adds an AI-assisted analysis layer.

    The traditional approach looks like this:

     

     
    Integration Failure
        ↓
Monitoring
        ↓
Message Processing Log
        ↓
Manual Investigation
        ↓
Root Cause
        ↓
Action
    The proposed approach is:

     

     
    Integration Failure
        ↓
Exception Subprocess
        ↓
Collect Error Context
        ↓
AI Adapter
        ↓
AI Incident Analysis
        ↓
Operational Notification
        ↓
Human Investigation / Action
    The AI provides the initial interpretation, while the existing monitoring capabilities remain available for detailed technical investigation.

    Use Case

    The use case is based on a Sales Order integration between an external application and SAP S/4HANA.

    The external application sends a Sales Order request to SAP S/4HANA through SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration.

    Under normal conditions, the integration processes the request and the Sales Order is created successfully.

    However, if an error occurs during the integration, the scenario follows a different path. Instead of simply reporting the technical failure, the integration captures the available error context and sends it to the AI Adapter for analysis.

    One important architectural principle here is that the AI processing only happens when an error occurs.

    The normal business flow does not need to invoke the AI model.

    This is an important point when thinking about AI in integration scenarios:

    AI does not necessarily need to be part of every transaction. It can be activated when intelligence is actually needed.

    Technology Components

    The solution combines several capabilities of the SAP ecosystem:

     

     

     

     

    The key point is that these components are combined into an incident-analysis flow, rather than using AI as part of every normal transaction.

    Setting Up SAP Generative AI Hub

    To implement this scenario, the AI capabilities are provided through SAP Generative AI Hub.

    The Generative AI Hub provides a governed environment for accessing generative AI models and incorporating them into enterprise scenarios.

    For this example, the AI model is used to analyze integration incidents and generate a structured troubleshooting response.

     

     

    The exact model configuration can vary depending on the available models and the customer's SAP environment.

    For this scenario, the important concept is not the specific model itself, but the ability to expose generative AI capabilities to the integration flow in a controlled way.

    Configuring the AI Adapter

    Once the AI environment is available, the next step is to configure the AI Adapter in SAP Cloud Integration.

    The AI Adapter is used to invoke the AI capabilities from within the integration flow.

     

     

     

     

     

     

     In the Service Key, the endpoint is provided under serviceurls as AI_API_URL. This value is used as the API endpoint when configuring the connection to SAP AI Core.

    OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials

    To connect SAP AI Launchpad and SAP Integration Suite to SAP AI Core, the required authentication information is obtained from a Service Key of the SAP AI Core service instance.

    In SAP BTP Cockpit, navigate to the subaccount where SAP AI Core is provisioned and open the corresponding SAP AI Core service instance.

    From the service instance, create a new Service Key and download or copy its credentials. 

    In this scenario, the AI Adapter is placed inside the Exception Subprocess.

    This is intentional.

    The AI service is not invoked for every successful Sales Order.

    It is invoked when an integration failure occurs and additional analysis is required.

    This creates an architecture where AI becomes an on-demand intelligence layer for integration incidents.

    Defining the AI Prompt

    The next step is defining what the AI should do with the integration error.

    Rather than asking a generic question such as:

    "What is wrong with this integration?"

    the prompt defines a structured troubleshooting task.

    For example:

     

     
    You are an SAP Integration troubleshooting assistant.

Analyze the following integration incident.

SAP S/4HANA Error:
${property.error_message}

MPL ID:
${property.mpl_id}

Provide the analysis using the following structure:

1. Incident Summary
2. Probable Root Cause
3. Business Impact
4. Evidence
5. Investigation Points
6. Recommended Actions
7. Can the message be safely reprocessed?
8. Priority Level
    The structure of the prompt is important.

    The goal is not simply to generate a natural-language answer.

    The goal is to produce an output that can be used by an integration operations or support team.

    Step 1 — Capture the Error Context

    The first step in the Exception Subprocess is to capture the relevant error information generated by the integration.

    For example, the HTTP layer may provide:

     

     
    Bad Request : 400 : HTTP/1.1
     

    However, the backend response can contain much more meaningful information:

     

     
    Material TG1100 is not defined for sales org. 1410,
distr. chan. 10, OrProperty 'SoldToParty' has invalid value '14100009000'

     

    The integration can extract the relevant error information and make it available to the AI analysis.

    This distinction is important.

    A generic HTTP status tells us:

    Something failed.

    The backend error can help explain:

    Why it failed.

    This is one of the key requirements for an AI-assisted monitoring scenario:

    The AI needs meaningful context, not just an HTTP status code.

    Step 2 — AI Analysis with the AI Adapter

    Once the relevant error context has been prepared, the Exception Subprocess invokes the AI Adapter.

    The AI receives the error information together with the instructions defined in the prompt.

    The goal is to transform a technical exception into a structured incident analysis.

    For example:

     

     
    Technical Error
       ↓
AI Adapter
       ↓
Generative AI Model
       ↓
Structured Incident Analysis
    This is where the solution starts moving from monitoring toward intelligent operations.

    Step 3 — Processing the AI Response

    The AI Adapter returns the generated incident analysis.
    The response can then be passed to the notification step, where it is included in the operational notification sent to the support or integration team.

     

     

     
    The result is no longer just:

     

     
    HTTP 400
    Instead, the support team receives a structured analysis.

    For example:

     

     
    1. Incident Summary:
Sales Order creation failed in SAP S/4HANA.

2. Probable Root Cause:
Material TG1100 is not maintained for sales organization
1410 and distribution channel 10.

3. Business Impact:
The Sales Order could not be created.

4. Evidence:
Material = TG1100
Sales Organization = 1410
Distribution Channel = 10

5. Investigation Points:
Verify the material master and sales area data.

6. Recommended Actions:
Extend the material to the required sales area or
use a valid material.

7. Can the message be safely reprocessed?
No. The master data issue should be corrected first.

8. Priority Level:
High.
    The important difference is that the system has moved from:

    Error Detection

    to:

    Contextual Analysis

    Step 4 — Turning AI Analysis into an Operational Notification

    Once the AI has analyzed the integration error, the result can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

    For this Proof of Concept, the AI-generated analysis is included in an automated notification.

     

    The important point is that the notification is not intended to replace the monitoring platform.

    It provides an AI-generated first analysis before the analyst starts the deeper investigation.

    In our example, the notification is sent by email. However, the same AI-generated analysis could also be delivered through other channels, such as Microsoft Teams, SAP Alert Notification service, or an IT service management platform.

    Where Could This Go Next?

    This approach opens several possibilities for extending AI-assisted integration monitoring and intelligent operations.

    Automatic Error Classification

    Errors could be classified into categories such as:

    • Authentication
    • Authorization
    • Connectivity
    • Mapping
    • Transformation
    • Master Data
    • Business Validation
    • Backend Errors
      Final Result

      Final Result

      After the integration failure is detected and analyzed, the AI-generated incident analysis can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

      In this example, the result is delivered by email. However, the same approach could be used to automatically create an incident or service ticket, send a notification through Microsoft Teams, or integrate with an IT service management platform.

      The important point is that the support team receives more than a technical error message. The AI provides a structured first analysis that can help the team understand the incident and decide what to investigate next.

      Example 1 — Invalid Material in SAP S/4HANA

       

      Example 2 — Invalid Business Partner in SAP S/4HANA

       

       

       

       

       

      Conclusion

      This could help operations teams prioritize and route incidents.

      When an integration fails, knowing that it failed is only the first step.

      The real challenge is understanding what happened, why it happened, and what should be investigated next.

      In this scenario, SAP Integration Suite, the AI Adapter, and SAP Generative AI Hub were combined to add an AI-assisted incident analysis layer to an existing integration monitoring process.

      The goal is not to replace monitoring, logs, or the expertise of integration teams. Instead, AI can help transform technical error information into a structured starting point for investigation and action.

      As integration landscapes continue to grow in complexity, this approach opens the door to a different way of thinking about integration operations:

      From detecting failures to understanding incidents.

      And perhaps the next step is not simply asking:

      "Did my integration fail?"

      but rather:

      "What happened, why did it happen, and what should I do next?"

       
      SAP Integration Suite
      Cloud Integration  
      SAP AI Core

entry.title: How We Built a Structured AI Readiness Assessment for SAP Customers - Stop Guessing. Start Assessing
entry.content:
Ask ten customers "how ready are you for AI?" and you get ten different answers — all of them based on gut feeling. Some point to a Copilot pilot that ran for three weeks. Others mention their data lake. A few say "we have an AI strategy" but can't tell you who owns it or what it covers. The result: conversations that start from completely different baselines, and recommendations that don't land.

That's the gap a structured AI Readiness Assessment closes.

We designed the assessment around nine dimensions — covering everything from executive strategy and workforce readiness to data foundation, technology infrastructure, and AI governance. Two dimensions are deliberately SAP-specific: the maturity of the SAP landscape itself, and whether there is an actual plan to consume and realize value from SAP's AI capabilities. Generic maturity frameworks miss exactly these.

Each dimension is scored 1–5: from L1 Initial (ad hoc, no structure) to L5 Autonomous Enterprise Ready (AI drives outcomes, full lifecycle in place). A score of 2 isn't a failure — it's a priority signal. What matters is the pattern across all nine axes: where is the organization strong, where is it lagging, and where are the critical gaps?

The assessment runs as a facilitated workshop, not a survey. When a cross-functional group has to agree on a number, the disagreements that surface are themselves a finding. That conversation produces three outputs.

The first is a radar chart — a 9-axis diagram showing current score in blue and target score in green for a 12–18 month horizon. The gap between the two lines is the prioritized action space.

The second is a gap analysis: for each dimension with a delta, concrete actions, ownership (SAP-side vs. customer-side), and effort classification — quick win or strategic initiative.


The third is a benchmark comparison — how does the customer's profile compare to peers at a similar transformation stage. This reframes the conversation from "are we good enough" to "where do we invest next to stay competitive."

 

The Tool Behind It
The assessment runs in a purpose-built Excel workbook with weighted scoring per dimension, plus a companion HTML visualization that renders the radar chart and gap analysis live during the session — no server, no login, no external dependency.

If you're working on something similar or want to adapt this for your own customer engagements, feel free to reach out.

entry.title: How Companies Are Approaching MCP: Reflections From Amsterdam
entry.content:
AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe took place in Amsterdam on 17–18 September 2026 as part of the Agentic AI Foundation’s community events. It brought together protocol maintainers, open-source contributors and enterprise engineering teams to discuss MCP and the infrastructure needed to put agents into practice. Across the keynotes and technical sessions, a recurring question was how open standards can help agents work with tools and services across different platforms.

As an architect in SAP’s Cross Product Alignment team, I work on MCP architecture and guidance. My work also includes contributing to the MCP Server Card initiative and discussions on discovery metadata as part of SAP’s contributions to the MCP community within the Agentic AI Foundation. The conference offered a chance to look beyond our own work at SAP and hear how companies are approaching integration, discovery and agent execution.

Putting MCP into practice involves more than connecting an agent to a tool. Teams are deciding how capabilities are discovered, what information enters the model’s context and how access is managed. These choices become increasingly important as MCP use grows from individual experiments into shared services.

 

A Protocol That Is Easier To Operate At Scale

 

The MCP protocol updates highlighted in the keynote addresses practical challenges in running MCP across distributed systems. The July 2026 revision of the protocol introduces a stateless core, replacing the initialization handshake and protocol-level sessions with protocol version and capability information carried on each request. This reduces the need to tie a client’s requests to a particular server instance. Applications can still retain business state through explicit handles.

Multi-round-trip requests address another operational concern: waiting for additional input. A server can return a request for information, allowing the client to gather it and resubmit the request with that information without keeping a stream open throughout the wait.

The revision also introduces cache hints for resource and capability responses, alongside standardized HTTP headers that make MCP operations more visible to infrastructure components.

Together, these changes support deployment through existing service infrastructure. Application state and safe retry handling remain implementation responsibilities, even when the protocol itself is stateless.

 

From Individual Integrations To Shared Infrastructure

 

The sessions on enterprise adoption explored how shared infrastructure can support MCP use across teams. The approaches presented combined catalogs, gateways and publishing processes to give teams a common way to discover, access and publish integrations while allowing developers to choose among supported agent clients.

An important part of this approach is the division of responsibility. Teams retain ownership of their integrations, while shared infrastructure provides connectivity, validation and publication checks. Making a server available also creates responsibilities for maintaining it, reviewing changes and helping others find it.

As organizations expose more capabilities, these responsibilities become harder to handle through individual configurations. Discovery metadata, ownership and access controls need to be considered as part of the integration from the beginning.

 

Progressive Tool Discovery And The Role Of The Harness

 

The discussions on context management highlighted an important distinction: loading every tool definition into model context upfront is a client implementation choice, rather than a requirement of MCP.

The harness coordinates the model, context and tool execution. It determines which tool information reaches the model and how intermediate results are handled. Progressive tool discovery allows a client to reveal capabilities gradually, retrieving detailed definitions when they become relevant to a task.

This can reduce the information loaded upfront, but discovery also has a cost. Additional searches or repeated attempts can offset the savings. The useful question is whether selective loading helps the agent complete its task reliably and efficiently.

Context management needs to be evaluated as part of the complete workflow. A smaller initial set of tool definitions can be useful, but the agent still needs to find the appropriate tools and use them correctly.

Progressive tool discovery compared with loading all tool definitions upfront. AI-generated conceptual illustration, reviewed by the author. It does not represent benchmark results.

 

 

How Tools Are Executed Matters Too

 

The conference discussions on tool execution also explored how command-line interfaces can work together with MCP. A related article on progressive discovery and shell composition illustrates how a CLI can use the harness’s existing MCP connections. This allows the agent to inspect available tools and filter their results through shell commands before returning the relevant information to the model.

This shows why MCP and CLI do not always need to be treated as competing choices. MCP can provide the connection to a capability, while a CLI or code execution environment provides a way to compose calls and process results.

An illustrative example of this pattern would be an agent summarising overdue invoices. Using a CLI connected to the harness’s MCP tools, it could retrieve invoice records and pass them to code that filters overdue items and calculates totals by customer and currency. In this setup, the execution environment could process the records and return only the resulting summary data to the model. MCP provides access to the tool, while the execution environment processes the data before the model writes the summary.

Discovery and execution therefore need to be considered together. How much information enters the model’s context? Which intermediate steps can be handled programmatically? Where are permissions enforced? Those choices help explain an integration’s behaviour beyond the interface used to invoke it.

 

Skills Bring Guidance Closer To Capabilities

 

The session on Skills over MCP was particularly interesting to me because it addresses what happens after a capability becomes available. A tool contract describes an operation and its inputs. A skill can provide workflow instructions, examples and supporting references that help an agent use several operations together.

The Skills over MCP extension allows servers to distribute these instructions and supporting files through MCP. Clients can discover skills and retrieve their contents when needed. The host remains responsible for how a skill is selected, loaded and presented to the model. Retrieving a file does not automatically activate it.

This creates an architectural question: which guidance should belong to the capability provider, and which decisions should remain with the harness?

The provider understands the service and its intended workflows. The harness manages the current task, available context and execution environment. Keeping that division explicit could help providers deliver useful guidance without assuming that every client behaves identically.

A related proposal discussed at the conference was applying semantic versioning to skills. Changes to instructions can change agent behavior, so those instructions also deserve lifecycle management.

 

Tool Discovery Starts Before The Connection

 

Progressive disclosure helps an agent select tools from available providers. In a larger landscape, there is an earlier question: how does the agent find the relevant provider in the first place?

@sebastian_wennemersand I explored this question in our session, “From API Catalogs to Agent Catalogs.” Through a spacecraft story and live demo, we showcased how Open Resource Discovery and MCP Server Cards can work together to support discovery before a client connects to a server.

ORD provides a way to publish and aggregate resource metadata, helping consumers find relevant MCP servers across a larger landscape. MCP Server Cards complement this by describing individual servers and how to connect to them. Together, they help address the discovery challenge at two levels: finding a relevant provider and understanding how to access it.

Since the conference, SEP-2127 on MCP Server Cards has reached Final status. Our demo also explored including tool metadata in the Server cards to help consumers assess relevance before connecting. This goes beyond the finalized design, with tool metadata being explored as future work in the Server Card community.

The audience was curious about how these pieces fit together and could be applied in practice. Those conversations reinforced the importance of making capabilities discoverable, alongside making them available.

 

What This Means For Developers And Architects

 

For teams building with MCP, the conference discussions suggest evaluating the full path from a user’s request to a completed task.

Can the agent find the appropriate provider? Does it receive the tool definitions and guidance it needs at the right time? Can the harness coordinate execution reliably, with clear permissions and ownership?

For organizations with mature APIs and integration infrastructure, there is another question: where does MCP improve interoperability across agent clients or make business capabilities easier to use? That benefit needs to justify the additional layer that teams will maintain.

These are practical questions to bring into architecture reviews and evaluations. Comparing complete workflows can help teams identify which choices actually improve the outcome.

Where is your team encountering the most difficulty: exposing capabilities, helping agents discover them, or making their use reliable within a workflow?

entry.title: How Account Synopsis and Executive Summary Work in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2
entry.content:
Smarter Account Intelligence in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2: Account Synopsis and Executive Summary

 

Why Account Context is Still a CX Problem

A seller has a customer meeting in 15 minutes.

The account record contains years of activity history, open opportunities, service interactions, stakeholder changes, and strategic account planning data.

Everything the seller needs is technically available, but finding what matters is a different challenge.

Meanwhile, on the service side, an agent picks up a call from a long-standing customer. The case history is there. The contracts are there. But the agent has no idea what this company actually does, what market they operate in, or whether there is an upsell opportunity sitting right in front of them.

This is one of the most common problems in modern customer-facing organizations; whether sales or service. Teams rarely struggle because they lack data. They struggle because important context is scattered across multiple sources and requires time to complete the puzzle.

As a result:

  • New account managers spend weeks getting up to speed.
  • Sales reps walk into meetings with incomplete context.
  • Service agents handle interactions without understanding the customer’s broader business.
  • Strategic account reviews become exercises in information gathering rather than strategy.
  • The gap is no longer data availability, but understanding.

This is exactly where Account Synopsis and Account Plan Executive Summary in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 enter the picture. Both use Generative AI to reduce the effort required to understand an account; yet they solve different problems, and they serve different audiences.

 

Two Features. Two Different Questions.

A useful way to understand these capabilities is to focus on the business question each one answers.

Account Synopsis

Account Synopsis answers: "Who is this customer and what is happening in their world?"

It combines publicly available company information with account master data to create a quick business briefing directly inside the Account record. The key word here is external: this feature reaches beyond your CRM to pull in market intelligence you would otherwise spend time Googling.

Account Synopsis is available in both SAP Sales Cloud V2 and SAP Service Cloud V2, but the use case differs by role:

  • For sales reps, it is a meeting preparation tool: building account context before discovery sessions, executive introductions, and account handovers.
  • For service agents, it is a real-time context layer: surfaced during customer interactions to help agents facilitate targeted conversations and identify upsell or cross-sell opportunities on the spot.

Account Plan Executive Summary (Sales Cloud V2 Only)

The Executive Summary answers: "What is our strategy for this account and how are we progressing?"

Instead of relying on external company information, it looks inward. It uses Account Plan content already maintained inside Sales Cloud: goals, SWOT analyses, action plans, business figures, and pipeline information to generate a concise strategic narrative.

This feature is specific to SAP Sales Cloud V2, because it is tied to Account Plans: a concept that lives in the sales planning workflow. It is not available in Service Cloud V2.

This makes it valuable for:

  • Quarterly Business Reviews
  • Strategic account reviews
  • Leadership briefings
  • Customer planning sessions

 

Where These Features Sit in SAP’s AI Strategy

SAP’s AI portfolio within Sales and Service Cloud V2 includes predictive Machine Learning, Generative AI capabilities, and the emerging layer of AI agents. Account Synopsis and Executive Summary sit firmly within the Generative AI category because their purpose is not prediction. Their purpose is synthesis.

Instead of trying to forecast future outcomes, they transform large amounts of information into structured narratives that humans can consume quickly. The goal is not to tell a seller or service agent what decision to make, but to help them reach a decision faster.

Both features are delivered as part of the Joule Premium for Customer Experience package and are embedded into SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 AI capabilities.

In practical terms: the intelligence behind these features is not some standalone AI experiment. It is deeply wired into the platform you are already using, whether that platform serves your sales team, your service team, or both.

 

A Closer Look at Account Synopsis

Opening an Account Synopsis generates a structured view of the customer across several configurable dimensions. Administrators can choose which of the following to expose to users:

  • Overall Information
  • Business Overview
  • Typical Customers
  • Competitive Landscape
  • Culture and Background
  • Business Strategies

 

 

Together, these sections create a quick overview of the organization that goes well beyond what is typically stored in CRM records. The AI consumes external, publicly available data about the company in real-time, delivering market intelligence as a structured synopsis directly in a dedicated AI Synopsis tab within the Account detail view. Each generation or regeneration counts as one AI unit transaction.

Sales Cloud and Service Cloud: Where the Value Lands

In SAP Sales Cloud V2, Account Synopsis is primarily a preparation tool. Sales reps use it before meetings, during account handovers, and as part of discovery sessions.

The value is measured in time saved during account planning: SAP’s benchmarks show a reduction from 60 minutes to 30 minutes per account review.

In SAP Service Cloud V2, the same synopsis is surfaced directly to service agents during live customer interactions. Here, the value is different: it is about enabling targeted conversations and spotting cross-sell or upsell opportunities in real-time. SAP’s published metrics point to a 2% increase in cross-sell and upsell revenue for service FTEs.

 

The Account Plan Executive Summary (Sales Cloud V2)

Many organizations invest significant time maintaining goals, SWOT analyses, revenue targets, action plans, and strategic initiatives, only to create separate documents when leadership reviews or QBRs arrive. If that sounds familiar, you are not alone.

The Executive Summary addresses this problem. Available exclusively in SAP Sales Cloud V2, it converts structured planning information into a concise narrative that can be reviewed, edited, and shared directly from within the Account Plan.

The generated output is organized around four themes:

Account Overview A summary of the customer relationship, strategic positioning, and business objectives.

Customer Priorities and Our Response An explanation of customer goals and how the organization is addressing them.

Risks and Challenges Known risks, dependencies, and potential obstacles.

What’s Upcoming Future engagements and relevant pipeline information.

 

How to Trigger It

Users navigate to Account Plans → open a plan → select the Executive Summary tab → choose “Generate Summary.” The result is an editable draft that can be copied to clipboard for external use. If a summary was previously generated, it can be viewed or regenerated.

Unlike Account Synopsis, the Executive Summary is fully editable. Users can refine the content, add business context, and save the final version directly inside the plan.

 

 

The following figures come from SAP’s Business AI Value Calculator (v3.6, June 2026) and published product pages on the SAP Discovery Center. These are SAP-validated benchmarks based on VLM (Value Lifecycle Management) benchmarks and SAP Expert Estimation.

The service-side value proposition is less about time savings and more about revenue capture. When agents understand the customer’s business context during a live interaction, they are better positioned to identify opportunities that would otherwise be invisible.

 

In the Field: Döhler’s Story

The most publicly documented live deployment is Döhler, a global food and beverage ingredients company with approximately 9,500 employees, €640 million+ in revenue, 3,000+ CRM users, and 27,600 customers. Döhler went live on SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 globally in Q3 2025.

Key facts from their deployment:

  • Account Synopsis is live in production alongside Lead Booster, Lead Intelligence/Scoring, Deal Scoring, Case Summary, Case Classification, and Similar Case Recommendation.
  • Integration with OpenAI was used to enrich leads and accounts, with market insights such as product shortages surfaced automatically.
  • The system delivers "exceptional loading speed and system responsiveness" with "virtually no loading times" even on large account/opportunity objects.

"The usability, performance and productivity gains are excellent. We are excited to deploy SAP’s Sales and Service Cloud V2 in 2025 expanding on the exceptional value to IT, end users, customers and suppliers."

— Vasiliki Galani, Lead IT & Market Functions, Döhler

 

Prerequisites and Licensing

Before activating these features, there are a few practical items to check off. This is the part of the article that saves you a support ticket.

Licensing: Both features require a valid SAP AI Units license: specifically the Joule Premium for Customer Experience package. This applies whether you are using Account Synopsis in Sales Cloud V2, Service Cloud V2, or both. Customers must raise an incident with component CEC-CRM-ML confirming their license to enable the features.

Role Assignment: Users need the sap.crm.service.mlScenarioManagementGenAIService role assignment.

Language Support: Generative AI features are tested and supported for English, German, French, and Spanish. Use in other languages is untested and may produce unreliable results. Human review is recommended.

AI Unit Consumption: Each Account Synopsis generation counts as one transaction. Every regeneration also counts as a separate transaction. The same applies to other GenAI features like Lead Booster, Email Drafter, and Survey Trend Summary.

⚠️Note: The Joule Premium for Customer Experience per-user-per-month SKU is currently being retired, as SAP is moving these features into Base AI. If you are signing a new contract or renewing, confirm with your SAP Account Executive whether Account Synopsis is covered under your Base AI entitlement or still requires a separate AI Units purchase before raising an activation incident.

 

Final Thoughts

The most successful AI capabilities in enterprise software are often the least disruptive.

They do not change how people work. They improve how quickly people can work.

Account Synopsis and Account Plan Executive Summary follow that principle.

Account Synopsis helps both sellers and service agents understand the customer’s world.

Executive Summary helps account teams communicate their strategy.

Neither replaces experience. Neither replaces account knowledge. And neither removes the need for good data.

But when implemented in the right environment with clean data, clear processes, and realistic expectations: both can reduce the distance between information and understanding.

Besides, if an AI can save you from one more “So... tell me about your company” moment - whether you are a seller in a boardroom or an agent on a call - I would say it has already earned its keep.

entry.title: t's All Joule Everywhere, Do You Actually Know Which Joule You are Talking About?
entry.content:
t's All Joule Everywhere, Do You Actually Know Which Joule You are Talking About?

Spend any time in the SAP ecosystem right now and you will hear one word more than any other and its Joule

Joule in SuccessFactors. Joule Work. Joule Agents. Joule Assistants. Joule Studio. It's on every slide in every keynote, in every product update. 

"Are these all the same thing? Are they different products? What does each one actually do, and which one do I actually need?"

Let's break it down.

Before the classification, it's worth asking: why does this family even exist?

For decades, enterprise software was designed around a fundamental assumption: users learn the system. You train people to navigate menus, find features, run reports, follow workflows. The system was the authority and users adapted to it.

The result? Feature-rich platforms where most users only ever discover 20% of the capability. Time-off requests, performance forms and policy questions are all buried inside screens that require navigation, training and patience.

The Joule Family: A Clear Classification

Think of the Joule family as a layered stack each layer serving a distinct purpose, all working together

Layer 1 — Joule (The Umbrella AI Experience)

What it is: Joule is SAP's overarching AI copilot and engagement layer. It is "the broader AI experience through which people interact with their business.

The need it addresses: Users need a single, consistent AI presence across SAP regardless of which module, which device, or which process they are working in. Joule is that presence.

Its function: Joule answers questions, provides recommendations, helps users navigate to the right application, and surfaces insights drawn from SAP and connected third-party data. It is grounded in the SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than 7 million data fields across the SAP portfolio giving it real business context, not generic AI responses.

Layer 2 — Joule Assistants (The Orchestrators)

What they are: Joule Assistants are purpose-built for a specific business role or process. They go beyond answering questions they coordinate the work that needs to happen within a defined business context.

The need they address: Generic AI can answer questions. But HR work is contextual. A payroll query and a workforce planning request are very different they need different data, different logic, different guardrails. Joule Assistants bring that role-specific intelligence.

its function: "The Assistant coordinates the work, while the Agent carries out the tasks needed to move it forward." Assistants understand the nuances of a process, surface the right context

Layer 3 — Joule Agents (The Executors)

What they are: Joule Agents are the doers. They execute multi-step tasks autonomously across systems, across data sources, within the boundaries set by your organisation's existing authorisations, rules and audit trails.

The need they address: Orchestration without execution is just planning. Once an Assistant decides what needs to happen, something has to do it update a record, trigger a workflow, move a configuration, generate a document across potentially multiple systems in sequence.

Their function: Agents carry out specific, bounded tasks. Critically, they operate within your existing governance they don't bypass permissions or create shadow workflows. SAP's framing is deliberate: "Agents operate within established data, authorisations, and audit trails to maintain control."

Layer 4 — Joule Work (The Workspace / UI)

What it is: Joule Work is the new unified interface "the new UI for AI" where employees and HR teams actually engage with all of the above. Launched at SAP Connect 2026 and rolling out to all customers in October 2026.

The need it addresses: Having powerful Assistants and Agents is only useful if people can actually reach them intuitively. Joule Work solves the access and discoverability problem it replaces navigation-first interaction with intent-first interaction.

Its function: Joule Work is built on three pillars:

  • Conversations - Users express what they want in natural language. Joule Work interprets the intent, engages the right Assistant, and gets the work done.
  • Spaces - Dynamic, shared work areas that surface the content, data, insights, and applications relevant to a goal - across SAP and non-SAP sources. Think of a Workforce Planning Space that brings together headcount data, open roles, skills gaps, and budget in one view.
  • Develop (Joule Studio) - The build capability, directly accessible within Joule Work, where teams extend or create their own agents and workflows.

 

Layer 5 — Joule Studio (The Build Layer)

 

What it is: Joule Studio is SAP's AI-first development environment. It enables business users and IT professionals to create, customise and govern AI agents and workflows from no-code to pro-code.

The need it addresses: No out-of-the-box agent library covers every organisation's unique HR processes. Companies need the ability to extend Joule to fit their specific workflows, policies, and data structures without building from scratch on a separate platform.

Its function: Joule Studio lets you describe what you want to build in plain language it translates your intent into product requirements and technical specifications, then helps implement the solution. Agents built in Studio can reason across SAP and non-SAP systems, invoke APIs, and integrate into governed enterprise workflows.

 

How It All Fits Together Here's the mental model that I find most useful:

You INTERACT in     →  Joule Work       (the workspace)

You TALK TO         →  Joule            (the AI experience)

It COORDINATES via  →  Joule Assistants (the orchestrators)

It EXECUTES via     →  Joule Agents     (the doers)

You CUSTOMISE with  →  Joule Studio     (the builder)

entry.title: Natural Language (NL) Over SAP Data: A Practical MCP Pattern for Joule Desktop & Pro-Code Agent
entry.content:
Introduction

Any S/4HANA OData API, standard or custom, can be exposed as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway and consumed by AI agents through two complementary paths: Joule Work Desktop for a direct, low-overhead experience, and a custom agent in Cloud Foundry that can be triggered in Joule SAP Build Work Zone for an orchestrated, reasoning-capable experience. 

To make it concrete, we applied it to SAP Production Revenue Accounting (PRA) data: a domain that is rich, complex, and mission-critical, and where the gap between the data and the people who need it is wide enough to make the pattern's value immediately visible. The solution is not PRA-specific. The same architecture applies to any standard or custom OData V4 service in S/4HANA: Finance, Plant Maintenance, Materials Management, Sales and Distribution, or any domain where business users need structured answers without writing queries or navigating transaction codes.

This blog walks through the architecture, the components, the implementation decisions, and the trade-offs behind the two access patterns we designed and deployed:

  1. Joule Work Desktop — connects directly to an custom MCP server published via SAP Integration Suite. Ideal for business users who want a direct AI interface to standard PRA revenue accounting tables.

  2. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone — routes through a custom AI agent on SAP Cloud Foundry that adds an intelligent reasoning layer. Ideal for business users already operating inside Work Zone.

Both patterns share the same backend: a custom OData V4 service exposing standard SAP PRA tables, published as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway.

A full end-to-end walkthrough has been recorded as a companion to this blog.

Solution Architecture

The architecture is deliberately generic. Swap out the PRA OData service for any other S/4HANA OData V4 endpoint and the rest of the pattern holds unchanged.

The solution exposes standard S/4HANA PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service (built on ABAP RAP), publishes them as governed MCP tools through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway, and surfaces them to business users via natural language either directly through Joule Work Desktop or through a custom AI agent embedded in SAP Build Work Zone.

Path 1 — Joule Desktop:

Desktop User → Joule Desktop → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Path 2 — Joule in Work Zone:

Web User → SAP Build Work Zone (Joule) → A2A → Custom Agent on CF → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Component Walkthrough

1. S/4HANA On-Premise — The Data Source

The data lives in a standard S/4HANA on-premise system. We exposed the standard PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service built using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The service exposes all 13 entity sets with proper navigation associations, enabling deep $expand queries across both the Document and Revenue Distribution branches. 

 

2. SAP Integration Suite — MCP Gateway

This is the integration layer that bridges the RAP OData service into the AI world.

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Server capability (part of the MCP Gateway feature, available with the Premium subscription) consumes the OData V4 service metadata and automatically generates MCP tool definitions for every operation. For our 13-entity service, this produced 41 MCP tools covering list queries, filtered reads, and navigation operations.

Why MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for AI tool discovery and invocation. By publishing our OData service as an MCP server, we make it consumable by any MCP-compatible client, including Joule Work Desktop, LangChain agents, or any future client, without changing the backend.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The Developer Hub within Integration Suite is used to publish the MCP server, generating the OAuth credentials that clients use to authenticate. It also provides discoverability within the organization: other developers can find and reuse the same MCP server without rebuilding the integration from scratch.

3. SAP Cloud Foundry — Custom Reasoning Agent

For the Work Zone path, we built a custom Python agent deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. This agent adds the reasoning layer that bridges Joule's natural language input to structured MCP tool calls.

The agent stack:

ComponentRole

a2a-sdk

Implements the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, exposing a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint that Joule can call

LangGraph + LangChain

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) loop: decides which MCP tools to call, in what order, based on the user's question

langchain-mcp-adapters

Loads MCP tools from Integration Suite at runtime and wraps them as LangChain 

LiteLLM / langchain-litellm

Routes LLM calls to SAP AI Core using the standard OpenAI-compatible interface

The ReAct pattern is important here. Rather than a single-shot query, the agent reasons iteratively: it reads the question, identifies which MCP tools are relevant, calls them, evaluates the results, and decides whether additional calls are needed before formulating the final answer. This is what makes it capable of answering multi-hop questions that require joining data from multiple PRA tables.

4. Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

Deployment uses the Joule CLI. The deploy command registers the custom agent as a Joule capability. By default, this deploys to standalone Joule.

To surface the agent inside SAP Build Work Zone, update the assistant type to sap_digital_Assistant. The Joule Admin Center (accessible by appending /admin to the Joule instance URL) allows you to verify the deployment and confirm the capability is active.

5. SAP Build Work Zone - Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

SAP Build Work Zone is the standard business user entry point. Joule is embedded natively in the Work Zone shell,  no separate app to open, no separate login.

6. Joule Work Desktop Experience

For users who prefer the Joule Work Desktop standalone experience, the integration is simpler: Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server. No custom agent, no A2A, no Cloud Foundry deployment required.

Conclusion

The architecture supports two distinct experiences from the same foundation. Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server no agent required giving business users a fast, lightweight path to query SAP data in natural language. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone routes through a custom AI agent deployed on BTP Cloud Foundry, adding multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and a governed conversational interface for broader business user adoption.

The architecture is composable by design. The OData V4 service, MCP server, reasoning agent, and Joule capability are independent layers each doing one thing well. Swap the data source and the pattern applies to any SAP domain. Complexity lives where it belongs: the OData layer owns the data model, MCP handles tool discoverability, LangGraph handles reasoning, and Joule handles the conversation.

Consider which of your OData APIs could benefit from this pattern  a Finance posting service, a Plant Maintenance feed, a Sales Order status endpoint. Any of them can become a natural language interface using exactly this stack.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.

entry.title: MCP and SAP Integration Part 4: Who Gets to Act?
entry.content:
Introduction

The first time my AI agent tried to create a sales order in SAP S/4HANA, my own server stopped it:

NOT_AUTHORIZED: This client is not allowed to run prepare_sales_order.Required scope: Orders.Write.

That refusal was the best result of the whole series.

Here is why. Until now, my agent could only read : customers, sales orders, delivery status .If it got something wrong, the worst case was a wrong answer. The moment an agent can write , a mistake becomes an order for 500 pumps instead of 50, or the same order twice because a request was retried. A reader put it perfectly in a comment on Part 1: "Tool availability should never be confused with execution authority." An agent that can find a tool should not automatically be allowed to use it. 

So in this post, I let the agent create its first sales order, but only after it gets past four checks. By the end, you will see it get refused, ask a human for permission, create the order, and prove that it really happened:

  1. A locked back door: The server validates the XSUAA token itself.
  2. Execution authority: Separate Read and Write scopes, checked for every tool.
  3. A human in the loop: A preview first, and the real action only after the user says yes.
  4. Proof and traceability: The result is read back, a retry never creates a duplicate, and every tool call leaves an audit line.

End-to-End Security Overview 

A request to create a sales order now passes four checks. Each one can stop it, and each stop is a clear, non-retryable answer the agent can explain.

Checks 2, 3 and 4 run in the MCP server, because only the server sees which tool is called. Every tool call there leaves one audit line.

Step 1: Lock the back door : 

Part 3 found a gap: the Cloud Foundry URL of the MCP server answered without any key or token. Anyone who found it could skip SAP API Management and read live S/4HANAdata. Before adding a write tool, that door had to close.

The fix: The MCP server validates the XSUAA token itself , with SAP's library @SAP/xssec. It checks the signature, issuer, expiry and audience: the same check theVerifyJWT policy does in API Management, now also inside the server. 

  • Bind the existing XSUAA instance to the app in manifest.yml 
services: - mcp-destination - mcp-xsuaa​
  • Install the library:
npm install @SAP/xssec​
  • Check every /mcp call before it reaches the MCP SDK:
async function authenticate(req) { try { const ctx = await createSecurityContext(authService, { req }); const t = ctx.token; return { ok: true, info: { clientId: t.clientId, scopes: t.scopes || [] } }; } catch (e) { return { ok: false, status: 401, error: "Unauthorized: a valid XSUAA token is required" }; }}​
  • /health stays open, because Cloud Foundry needs it. On Cloud Foundry, a missing XSUAA binding never means "open": the server refuses every call with 503 instead.

The Result 

Step 2: Who may run which tool 

A valid token proves who is calling. It says nothing about what the caller may do. Until now, the token carried only one scope, uaa.resource .

Why the check belongs in the MCP server. MCP sends every tool call as a POST to the same /mcp endpoint, and the tool name sits inside the JSON body. API Management sees who is calling. Only the MCP server sees which tool is being called.

  • Define two scopes in xs-security.json : The client gets only Read for now: 
{ "xsappname": "<your xsappname, without the !t... part>", "tenant-mode": "shared", "scopes": [ { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Read", "description": "Read customers and sales orders" }, { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Write", "description": "Prepare and create sales orders" } ], "authorities": [ "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Read" ]}​
cf update-service mcp-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

authorities decides which scopes the client-credentials token receives. The xsappnamemust match your existing instance:
cf env <app> shows it once XSUAA is bound.

  • My first attempt failed with "Cannot change tenant mode with update… from shared to dedicated". The tenant mode is fixed when the XSUAA instance is created, so check it before writing the file.
  • Check the token : A new token now carries the scope :
uaa.resourcena-63002c5d-...!t718802.Orders.Read​

  • Every tool declares its scope, and one check runs before any tool:
const scope = tool.scope || "Orders.Read";if (!hasScope(extra?.authInfo, scope)) { return toolError({ error: "NOT_AUTHORIZED", retryable: false, message: `This client is not allowed to run ${tool.name}. Required scope: ${scope}.` });}​

Read tools need Orders.Read. The new write tools, prepare_sales_order and confirm_sales_order , need Orders.Write .

The result: visible, but not allowed : 

With a Read-only token, I asked Cline:

"Create a sales order for customer 17100001: 3 pieces of material TG13".

Cline found prepare_sales_order in the tool list and called it. The server refused:

{ "error": "NOT_AUTHORIZED", "retryable": false, "message": "This client is not allowed to run prepare_sales_order. Required scope: Orders.Write."}

Cline explained it clearly: the connection can read orders but not create them, and "no order was created, the preparation step was blocked before anything happened." Because of retryable: false , it did not try again.

The server's own log shows who said no: ERR Tool prepare_sales_order refused: client sb-na-63002c5d-...!t718802 lacks scope Orders.Write .

The tool is available, but the agent has no authority to run it.

Cline suggested asking the "SAP API Management administrator" for the missing permission. That is slightly off, because the scope lives in XSUAA. The server decides; the agent only explains, and its explanation is a guess based on the error text. 

Step 3: A human in the loop : 

With Orders.Write added to authorities (and one more cf update-service), the client may create orders. But an agent that may write should still not write on its own. So creating an order takes two tools: 

The server alone cannot prove that a human said yes: The model could call confirm_sales_order by itself. So the human check has two layers on the client side as well:

  • Cline asks before every tool call : In Cline, under Auto-approve, untick Use MCP servers.
  • A rule in .clinerules :
## Creating sales orders- To create a sales order, first call prepare_sales_order and show the preview to the user.- Never call confirm_sales_order unless the user has seen that preview and replied "yes" in this conversation.- After confirm_sales_order, report the order number, status and whether it was verified. If the mode is "simulated", say so.​

The flow in Cline. I asked for the same order again. Cline returned a preview: customer17100001 (Domestic US Customer 1), material TG13, 3 PC, sales area 1710 / 10 / 00, order type OR. It added: "Nothing has been created yet. Do you confirm? Please reply yes."

Only after I typed yes did Cline call confirm_sales_order.

The rules guide the agent. The server enforces.

What confirms the business outcome?: 

An HTTP 201 proves that a request was accepted. It does not prove that the order exists in the state the user asked for. So
confirm_sales_order never answers from the POST response alone. After creating the order, it reads the order back and returns what the system actually holds, plus verified: true : 

{ "salesOrder": "SIM0000001", "customer": "17100001", "material": "TG13", "quantity": "3 PC", "status": "Open", "verified": true, "mode": "simulated - the SAP Business Accelerator Hub sandbox does not save new orders"}

Cline answered from that verified result:
"The sales order has been created: SIM0000001,customer 17100001, TG13, 3 PC, status Open, verified: yes."

Let's take one example here : When the server sends a create request (a POST) to SAP, SAP answers with a status code. 201 = “Created”, which basically means “I received your request and accepted it.”

“Accepted” is not the same as “exactly what you asked for”. It’s like ordering food: the waiter says “Order received!” (that’s the 201), but you only know your order is right when the plate arrives and you check it. Between the request and the result, things can differ:

  • SAP may fill in default values you didn’t send.
  • A field may be ignored or changed.
  • An item may be missing, or the order may be blocked later.

If the agent tells the user “Done!” based only on the 201, it may be reporting something that isn’t true.

Cline built its answer from the verified read-back, not from the request. So the user sees what the system really holds: order SIM0000001, customer 17100001, TG13, 3 PC, status Open, verified: yes.

Stated honestly: this order is simulated : The Business Accelerator Hub sandbox does not save new orders, so on the sandbox the write runs in a clearly labelled simulated mode, and Cline said so in its answer. With WRITE_MODE: live and the destination pointing to areal S/4HANA system, the same code does a real POST to A_SalesOrder (the SAP Cloud SDK fetches the CSRF token) and reads the new order back through the same API.

"Done" is a claim. "Verified" is a fact read back from the system. 

Retries without duplicates : 

In Part 3, a wrong retryable flag made the agent repeat a broken read six times. For reads that is annoying. For writes it is  dangerous: a retried "create" can mean two orders. So confirm_sales_order is idempotent. The server remembers the result for each confirmation Id . A second confirm with the same ID returns the first result and creates nothing.

I tested it by asking Cline: "Please confirm that order again."
The answer: "Confirmed, it's the same order, no duplicate was created: SIM0000001. Note: Already created earlier, no second order was created."

The other confirm cases are refused just as clearly:

All of them are marked retryable: false, so the agent stops and explains instead of looping.

Traceability: who called what, when, and what happened : 

In Part 1, I asked how an integration team would answer these questions once AI agentscall SAP: Which agent made the request? Which tool did it use? Where did it fail? How long did it take? Part 4 answers them with one audit line per tool call
.

  • API Management creates the ID: An Assign Message policy, the first step in Proxy Endpoint Pre Flow, adds a correlation ID to every request:
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt"> <Add> <Headers> <Header name="X-Correlation-ID">{messageid}</Header> </Headers> </Add> <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>true</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> <AssignTo createNew="false" type="request"/></AssignMessage>

The Debug Viewer shows it on the request sent to the MCP server, for example X-Correlation-ID: us10-trial-nonasg-router2-1054008-1330786-2.

 

  • The MCP server writes one AUDIT line per tool call : with that ID, the client, the tool, therequired scope, the decision and the outcome:
AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"get_order_updates","scope":"Orders.Read","decision":"allowed","outcome":"ok","ms":814}AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"prepare_sales_order","scope":"Orders.Write","decision":"allowed","outcome":"ok","ms":441}AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"confirm_sales_order","scope":"Orders.Write","decision":"allowed","outcome":"created SIM0000001","ms":1}

A refused call gets a line too, with "decision" :"refused" and "outcome":"NOT_AUTHORIZED"

To follow one request from the gateway to the server, take the ID from the Debug Viewer and search for it:

cf logs sap-mcp-server --recent | Select-String "<correlation id>"

"One request, one ID, from the gateway to the server log."

The reader's questions, answered : 

Tool availability is not execution authority. Now it is not just a principle, it is a check that runs on every call.

Wrapping Up : 

Over four posts, the same MCP server went from an idea, to a secured gateway, to live S/4HANA data, and now to an agent that may act, but only within clear limits. Cline, SAP API Management and the questions never changed. What changed is who may do what, and how we know what happened.
What I learned in this part:

  • A gateway needs a locked back door: The server must validate the token itself.
  • Authorization belongs where the tool name is visible: API Management knows who is calling; only the MCP server knows which tool.
  • Permissions can change without code: Moving from Read to Read and Write was one line in xs-security.json.
  • Split every write into prepare and confirm: The preview costs one extra message and buys a human decision.
  • Make writes safe to retry: The same confirmation must never create a second order.
  • Log every decision with one ID: It turns "what did the agent do?" into a search.

Discovery opens the door. Authorization decides who acts. Verification proves it happened.

Thank you to the reader whose comment on Part 1 turned this series into something much more useful than I first planned.

Related resources :

  • GitHub repository: sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev).
  • Part 1:MCP and SAP Integration: Connecting AI Agents with Enterprise APIs
  • Part 2 : MCP and SAP Integration from concept to practice. Part 2
  • Part 3 : MCP and SAP Integration Part 3: Live S/4HANA Data and Who Gets to Act.
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub
  • Model Context Protocol
  • Cline
